pis.title: Economics and economic activities
plain: Economics is the study of how people, businesses and governments choose to use limited resources to satisfy wants that never run out. That gap between limited resources and unlimited wants is scarcity, and it is why every choice has a cost.

The cost of a choice is its opportunity cost: the value of the next-best option you gave up. Economic activity is everything people do to produce, exchange (distribute) and consume goods and services. Microeconomics studies individual decision makers such as a household, a bank or a business; macroeconomics studies the whole economy, such as inflation, unemployment and GDP.
Every society answers three basic economic questions: what to produce, how to produce it, and for whom. How a country answers them defines its economic system.
key: Scarcity: resources (money, time, workers, materials) are limited compared with wants.
Opportunity cost = the next-best alternative given up, not every alternative.
Economic activities: production, distribution/exchange, consumption.
Microeconomics = individual households and firms; macroeconomics = the whole economy.
Trade-offs are made at the margin: one more hour, one more dollar, one more worker.
fin: A financial plan is an economics problem: limited income, many goals. Advisors help clients rank goals and see opportunity costs.
Banks allocate scarce capital: every dollar lent to one borrower can't be lent to another, so they price loans by risk.
Time is a scarce resource too: money invested early has more time to compound.
ex: Opportunity cost in numbers: $200 a month spent on eating out for 10 years, if invested at a 7% annual return instead, would grow to about $34,600 (future value of a monthly annuity).
Micro vs macro: a credit union deciding its CD rate is a micro decision; the Federal Reserve setting the federal funds target range (3.75%-4.00% after Sept. 16, 2026) is macro (Federal Reserve).
Scarcity at work: when gasoline spiked above $4.50 a gallon in spring 2026, households cut other spending to pay for fuel (BLS CPI releases, 2026).
pis.trap: Scarcity is not the same as a shortage. Scarcity is permanent and affects everything; a shortage is temporary and happens when a price is held below the market level. Also, opportunity cost is only the single next-best option, not the sum of everything you gave up.
pis.say: "Every dollar our client spends has an opportunity cost. The $200 a month going to takeout could be about $34,600 in ten years if it were invested, so we'll help them decide which goal deserves it."

qs.q: Why should our client care about economics when making personal money decisions?
qs.a: Because every money decision is a trade-off between limited income and many goals. Economics gives us the tool to compare them: opportunity cost. For example, $200 a month spent on takeout could grow to about $34,600 in ten years at 7%. When our client sees the real cost of each choice, they can put money where it matters most, like the emergency fund and retirement plan we recommended.

qs.q: What is the real cost of this decision for our client?
qs.a: The real cost is the opportunity cost: what they give up by choosing this option over the next-best one. The price tag is only part of it. If our client spends $5,000 of savings on an upgrade now, the cost is also the growth that money would have earned and the safety cushion it would have provided. That's why we suggest keeping the emergency fund intact and paying for the upgrade from a savings goal over the next ten months.

cards: Resources are limited while wants are unlimited, so people must make choices.
Even a millionaire faces scarcity of time.
The value of the next-best alternative given up when you make a choice.
Spending $5,000 on a car means giving up the growth that $5,000 could have earned.
Micro studies individual households and firms; macro studies the whole economy (GDP, inflation, unemployment).
A bank's CD rate is micro; the Fed's rate decision is macro.

pis.title: Economic resources (factors of production)
plain: Economic resources, also called factors of production, are the inputs used to make goods and services. There are four: land (natural resources such as soil, water, oil and minerals), labor (human effort, physical and mental), capital (human-made tools, buildings, machines and technology used to produce other goods) and entrepreneurship (the vision and risk-taking that combines the other three).

Each resource earns an income: land earns rent, labor earns wages, capital earns interest and entrepreneurs earn profit. Economists separate capital goods (the equipment itself) from financial capital (the money used to buy it). Human capital is the knowledge and skill a worker builds through education and training, and it raises the value of labor.
key: Land = natural resources; labor = human work; capital = human-made tools used in production; entrepreneurship = organizing and risk-taking.
Payments: rent, wages, interest, profit.
Capital goods vs financial capital: banks supply the money that buys capital goods.
Human capital: education and skills that make labor more productive.
Resources are scarce, so how they are combined decides how much a business can produce.
fin: Banks and investors supply financial capital, and lending decisions are really about whether a borrower will use resources productively.
Student loans and 529 plans finance human capital.
A business plan for a loan should show all four resources: location (land), staff (labor), equipment (capital) and the owner's experience (entrepreneurship).
ex: Human capital pays: in 2024, median weekly earnings were about $1,543 for workers with a bachelor's degree versus about $930 for those with only a high school diploma (BLS, 'Education pays').
Capital investment: a food truck owner who buys a second truck with an SBA 7(a) loan is turning financial capital into a capital good (SBA 7(a) loans go up to $5 million).
Land matters even for services: a bank branch's location affects how many customers it reaches.
pis.trap: Economists separate capital goods (tools, machines, buildings) from the financial capital (money) that buys them, but DECA exam questions often group money with capital resources, so if the choices are land, labor, capital and entrepreneurship, money belongs under capital. Also, entrepreneurship is a separate resource, not just another kind of labor.
pis.say: "To grow, this business needs all four economic resources: the right location, trained staff, equipment, and the owner's leadership. Our loan provides the financial capital to buy the equipment, which makes the owner's labor more productive."

qs.q: What resources does this business need, and how would you finance them?
qs.a: It needs all four factors of production: land, meaning a location; labor, meaning trained staff; capital, meaning equipment; and the owner's entrepreneurship. The scarcest one here is capital: the owner can't serve more customers without a second oven. So we'd finance that equipment with a term loan matched to the equipment's useful life, such as a five-year SBA 7(a) loan, so the extra sales the oven creates help pay for it.

qs.q: Is college worth it for our client's child?
qs.a: For most students, yes, because education builds human capital, which raises lifetime earnings. In 2024, workers with a bachelor's degree earned a median of about $1,543 a week versus about $930 with a high school diploma, according to the BLS. The key is the cost: we'd start a 529 plan now, compare in-state and community college options, and avoid borrowing more than the expected first-year salary.

cards: Land, labor, capital and entrepreneurship: the four resources used to produce goods and services.
Human-made goods such as tools, machines and buildings used to produce other goods and services.
A bakery's oven is capital; the loan that buys it is financial capital.
The knowledge, skills and experience that make a worker more productive.
Education and training raise human capital and earnings.

pis.title: Economic goods and services
plain: An economic good is a tangible product people want that is scarce enough to have a price, such as a car or a laptop. A service is an intangible activity performed for someone, such as a haircut, a tax return or financial advice. Free goods, like air, are not scarce, so they have no price.

Services have four characteristics that change how they are sold: they are intangible (you can't see or touch them before buying), inseparable (produced and consumed at the same time, often with the provider present), perishable (an empty appointment slot can't be stored and sold later) and variable (quality depends on who provides it and when). Most financial products, from a checking account to investment advice, are services.
key: Goods are tangible; services are intangible.
Services: intangible, inseparable, perishable, variable.
Economic goods are scarce and have a price; free goods are not scarce.
Consumer goods are bought by households; capital goods are used by businesses to produce.
Most U.S. jobs are in service-providing industries.
fin: Because financial services are intangible, customers judge them by trust signals: licenses, reviews, clear statements, a good app, a professional advisor.
Variability is why banks train staff with scripts and standards so every branch gives the same experience.
Perishability: an advisor's unused meeting hours are lost, so firms use online booking and webinars to fill capacity.
ex: About 4 in 5 U.S. jobs are in service-providing industries such as health care, finance, retail and hospitality (BLS Employment Situation, industry data).
Making a service tangible: banks hand clients printed plans, charts and statements, and apps show balances in real time, so customers can 'see' what they bought.
Inseparability: a financial advisor's meeting is produced and consumed at the same time, which is why the advisor's communication skills are part of the product.
pis.trap: Don't call a bank account or an insurance policy a 'good' because it comes with a card or a document. The card is just evidence; what you're buying is the service. Also, a free good has no price because it isn't scarce, not because someone gives it away.
pis.say: "Financial advice is a service, so our client can't touch it before buying. That's why we'll make it tangible: a one-page plan, a chart of their goals and a 90-day check-in."

qs.q: How do you sell something customers can't see or touch?
qs.a: You make the intangible tangible and build trust. Financial services are intangible, so customers look for proof. We'd show a one-page written plan, real numbers like the FDIC's $250,000 insurance limit, client reviews and our credentials. For example, a bank can show a savings goal tracker in its app so the customer sees progress every week. That turns a promise into something our client can check, which makes them more likely to stay.

qs.q: Why do you think customers switch banks?
qs.a: Because a bank's product is a service, and services are judged by the experience, which can vary. Customers leave after poor service, surprise fees or a clunky app, not usually over a small rate difference. For example, many banks now drop overdraft fees and offer early direct deposit to keep customers. So our plan focuses on consistent service: trained staff, clear fees and a mobile app that works, which keeps our client's customers loyal.

cards: A good is a tangible product with a price because it is scarce; a service is an intangible activity performed for someone.
A laptop is a good; tax preparation is a service.
An empty advisor appointment slot is lost forever: perishable.
Something so plentiful that it has no price because it is not scarce.
Air is a free good; bottled air would be an economic good.

pis.title: Economic utilities created by business
plain: Utility is the usefulness or satisfaction a product provides. Businesses add value by creating five types of economic utility: form utility (changing raw materials into a finished product), place utility (making a product available where customers want it), time utility (making it available when they want it), possession utility (making it easy to own, such as through credit or financing) and information utility (telling customers what they need to know to buy and use it).

Production creates form utility; marketing and distribution create most of the others. Customers pay for utility, which is why a service that saves time or travel can charge a fee even when the underlying product is the same.
key: Form: making or changing the product.
Place: getting it to where the customer is.
Time: having it available when the customer wants it.
Possession: making ownership possible (financing, easy payment).
Information: labels, statements, advice and education.
fin: Banks create time utility with 24/7 apps and ATMs, place utility with mobile check deposit and branches, possession utility with loans and credit, and information utility with statements, alerts and financial education.
A fund manager creates form utility by packaging hundreds of stocks into one index fund share.
Advisors mainly create information utility, which is why clear explanations are part of the product.
ex: Possession utility: a car loan lets a buyer drive the car today and pay over five years.
Time and place utility: mobile check deposit lets customers deposit checks from home at midnight instead of visiting a branch during business hours.

Form utility in finance: an S&P 500 index fund turns 500 separate stocks into a single product anyone can buy, often with fractional shares at brokerages such as Fidelity and Schwab (company account features).
pis.trap: Don't mix up place and time utility. Place is about where (a branch, an app, delivery to your door); time is about when (open 24/7, same-day service). One feature can create both, so name each one separately in your answer.
pis.say: "Our plan adds utility for customers: time utility with 24/7 mobile access, place utility because they never need to visit a branch, and information utility with simple savings alerts. That's value customers will pay for."

qs.q: Why would a customer pay for this service instead of doing it themselves?
qs.a: Because the service creates utility they value more than the fee. It saves time, brings the service to where they are, and gives them information they don't have. For example, a tax preparer creates information utility and saves hours, and a mistake could cost more than the fee. So we'd price the service by the time and risk it saves our client's customers, and show that value clearly in the marketing.

qs.q: How can our bank add value without lowering rates?
qs.a: By adding utility instead of cutting price. We can create time utility with 24/7 support and instant transfers, place utility with mobile deposit, possession utility with fast loan approvals, and information utility with spending insights and alerts. Customers often pick convenience over a slightly better rate. That protects the bank's profit margin while giving customers a reason to stay and bring more of their money.

cards: Value added by changing the form of materials into a finished product.
An index fund packages 500 stocks into one share.
Time: available when customers want it. Place: available where customers want it.
Value added by making it easier to own a product, such as through financing or easy payment.
A car loan lets you own the car now and pay later.

pis.title: Types of economic systems
plain: An economic system is the way a society answers the three economic questions: what to produce, how, and for whom. There are four types. A traditional economy relies on customs and habits passed down through generations. A command (planned) economy lets the government decide what is produced, how and at what prices. A market economy leaves those decisions to buyers and sellers through supply, demand and prices. A mixed economy combines market freedom with government involvement.

Every real economy is mixed; the difference is the balance. The United States is a mixed economy that leans toward the market: private businesses make most decisions, but government regulates, taxes, insures bank deposits and provides programs like Social Security. North Korea is close to pure command, while China calls its system a socialist market economy, with large state-owned companies and banks alongside private firms.
key: Traditional: customs decide.
Command: government decides.
Market: buyers and sellers decide through prices.
Mixed: a blend; the U.S. leans market.
Systems differ in property rights, freedom of choice and the role of government.
fin: In a market economy, interest rates and stock prices are set mostly by markets, with the Federal Reserve influencing short-term rates.
Investing abroad means accepting different rules: in command-leaning economies, the government can change prices, block payments or take control of companies.
Deposit insurance (FDIC) and securities rules (SEC) are examples of the 'mixed' part of the U.S. system.
ex: State-owned banking: China's largest banks, such as ICBC, are majority state-owned and are among the largest banks in the world by assets.

System risk for investors: after Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022, sanctions and Russian capital controls left foreign investors unable to sell Russian holdings, and MSCI removed Russia from its emerging-markets indexes (MSCI, 2022).
Government in a mixed economy: the FDIC has insured U.S. bank deposits since 1933 (FDIC).
pis.trap: Don't say the U.S. is a pure market or capitalist economy. It is mixed, with a market lean. And 'mixed' doesn't mean half-and-half: almost every country is mixed, at different points along the spectrum.
pis.say: "The U.S. is a mixed economy: markets set most prices, but the government steps in with protections like FDIC insurance. That combination is why our client's insured deposits are safe even if a bank fails."

qs.q: Why is the U.S. called a mixed economy?
qs.a: Because it combines market decisions with government involvement. Private businesses and consumers decide most of what is produced and what it costs, but the government regulates, taxes and runs programs. For example, the market sets loan rates, while the FDIC insures deposits up to $250,000 and the SEC regulates investments. For our client, that means they get the choice and competition of a market plus legal protections when something goes wrong.

qs.q: Would you invest in a country with a command economy?
qs.a: Only a small amount, and only through a diversified fund, because government control adds risk the market can't price well. In a command-leaning economy, the state can block payments, change rules or take over companies. For example, investors in Russian stocks in 2022 couldn't sell when sanctions and capital controls hit, and MSCI dropped Russia from its indexes. So for our client, we'd keep international exposure in a broad fund rather than betting on one country.

cards: An economic system where the government decides what to produce, how and for whom.
North Korea is close to a pure command economy.
An economic system where buyers and sellers make decisions through supply, demand and prices.
Prices act as signals instead of government orders.
A blend of market freedom and government involvement; every real economy is mixed.
The U.S. leans market but has FDIC insurance and Social Security.

pis.title: Supply and demand
plain: The law of demand says that when the price of a product rises, buyers want less of it, and when the price falls, they want more (all else equal). The law of supply says that when the price rises, sellers offer more, and when it falls, they offer less. The market price settles where the quantity buyers want equals the quantity sellers offer: the equilibrium price.

If the price is above equilibrium, there is a surplus and sellers cut prices. If it is below, there is a shortage and prices rise. A change in price moves along a curve; a change in something else shifts the whole curve. Demand shifts with income, tastes, the price of related goods, expectations and the number of buyers. Supply shifts with input costs, technology, the number of sellers, government rules and expectations.
Interest is the price of money. The demand for loans and the supply of savings set rates in credit markets, with the Federal Reserve influencing the short-term level.
key: Law of demand: price up, quantity demanded down.
Law of supply: price up, quantity supplied up.
Equilibrium: where supply meets demand.
Shortage (price too low) vs surplus (price too high).
Movement along a curve = price change; shift of the curve = other factors.
fin: Stock prices move with the supply of and demand for shares: good news raises demand.
Banks compete for the supply of deposits: when they need deposits to fund loans, they raise savings and CD rates.
Housing: few homes for sale plus steady demand keeps prices high even when mortgage rates rise.
ex: Supply shock: bird flu cut the number of egg-laying hens, and the average U.S. price of a dozen Grade A eggs hit a record of about $6.23 in March 2025 (BLS average price data).
Housing lock-in: many owners with mortgages below 4% chose not to sell when rates rose toward 7%, shrinking supply; the 30-year rate averaged about 7.11% in mid-November 2026 (Freddie Mac).
Price of money: when the Fed raised its target range to 3.75%-4.00% in September 2026, loan and deposit rates followed (Federal Reserve).
pis.trap: Don't say 'demand went up because the price went down.' That's a change in quantity demanded, a movement along the curve. Demand itself shifts only when something other than price changes, like income or tastes.
pis.say: "Home prices are high because supply is low: owners with 3% mortgages aren't selling. That won't change quickly, so we'd plan our client's purchase around today's prices and refinance later if rates fall."

qs.q: Why are home prices still so high even with mortgage rates around 7%?
qs.a: Because supply has stayed low while demand held up. Higher rates should cool demand, but they also stopped many owners from selling, since they don't want to give up mortgages below 4%. Fewer homes for sale means buyers compete for limited inventory, which keeps prices up. With the 30-year rate near 7.11% in November 2026, our client should budget for today's prices, keep the payment under about 28% of gross income and plan to refinance if rates drop.

qs.q: If our bank raises its savings rate, what happens?
qs.a: We'd attract more deposits, because a higher price for savings increases the quantity of money customers supply to us. That follows the law of supply. The trade-off is cost: paying more on deposits squeezes our margin unless we lend that money out profitably. For example, online banks pay higher rates because they have no branches. So we'd raise rates only on a promotional CD or high-yield account targeted at new money, not on every account.

cards: As price rises, quantity demanded falls, and as price falls, quantity demanded rises, all else equal.
Higher concert prices mean fewer tickets sold.
The price where quantity supplied equals quantity demanded.
Above it: surplus. Below it: shortage.
A price change moves along the curve; other factors (income, tastes, costs) shift the whole curve.
A raise in income shifts demand right.

pis.title: Functions of prices in markets
plain: In a market economy, prices do the work that government orders do in a command economy. Prices perform several functions. They ration scarce goods: a high price limits buyers to those who value the product most. They signal information: rising prices tell producers to make more and consumers to look for substitutes. They provide incentives: higher prices encourage sellers to supply more and buyers to conserve. They measure value: price expresses what something is worth in money so different things can be compared.

Prices also help balance supply and demand, moving toward equilibrium. Interest rates are prices too. A higher interest rate rations credit to borrowers who are less risky or who need it most, and signals savers to save more.
key: Rationing: price limits who buys a scarce product.
Signals: price changes tell producers and consumers what is happening.
Incentives: higher prices encourage more production and less use.
Measure of value: prices let us compare different things.
Interest rates are the price of borrowing; credit scores affect that price.
fin: Risk-based pricing: lenders charge higher rates to borrowers with lower credit scores, because the price covers the greater risk of default.
Fed rate hikes raise the price of money to cool spending and fight inflation.
Fees are prices: a bank's fee structure signals which behaviors it wants (direct deposit, minimum balances).
ex: Prices as signals: when gasoline topped $4.50 a gallon in spring 2026, drivers cut back and demand for fuel-efficient cars rose (BLS CPI releases, 2026).
Incentive pricing: rideshare surge pricing raises fares at busy times so more drivers come online and some riders wait.
Price of money: the Fed raised its target to 3.75%-4.00% in September 2026 to slow spending while inflation ran at 3.7% (Federal Reserve; BLS).
pis.trap: Don't say prices only exist to make profit. Their economic job is to ration, signal and motivate. And a price ceiling (like a cap on rent) stops the price from rationing, which is why shortages appear.
pis.say: "Interest is just the price of money. Our client's 680 credit score means a higher price for a car loan, so raising the score first could save them hundreds of dollars."

qs.q: Why does our client with a lower credit score pay a higher interest rate?
qs.a: Because the interest rate is the price of borrowing, and it reflects risk. A lower score signals a higher chance of missed payments, so lenders charge more to cover expected losses. That's risk-based pricing. On a $25,000 five-year car loan, even a few points of APR can cost well over $1,000. So before our client applies, we'd spend a few months lowering credit utilization and setting up autopay to earn a better price.

qs.q: Should our bank charge the same fee to everyone?
qs.a: Not necessarily, because prices send signals and create incentives. A fee waived for customers with direct deposit or a minimum balance encourages the behavior that makes accounts profitable. For example, many banks waive monthly fees with direct deposit. But fees must be clear and fair, or customers leave and regulators step in. We'd recommend a simple, transparent fee that's waived for easy-to-meet behaviors, so customers can avoid it.

cards: Price limits who can buy a scarce product to those willing and able to pay.
High concert ticket prices ration limited seats.
Price changes give buyers and sellers information about supply and demand.
Rising gas prices signal drivers to conserve.
Charging higher interest rates to borrowers with higher default risk.

pis.title: Competition
plain: Competition is the rivalry among businesses to sell to the same customers. It pushes firms to lower prices, raise quality, innovate and serve customers better. Price competition means winning on price; non-price competition means winning on quality, service, convenience, brand or features.

Economists describe four market structures. Pure (perfect) competition has many sellers of identical products and no control over price. Monopolistic competition has many sellers of similar but differentiated products, like restaurants. An oligopoly has a few large firms that watch each other closely, like airlines or wireless carriers. A monopoly has one seller with no close substitutes. Government uses antitrust laws, starting with the Sherman Act of 1890, to keep markets competitive.
key: Price vs non-price competition.
Market structures: pure competition, monopolistic competition, oligopoly, monopoly.
Competition benefits consumers: lower prices, better quality, more choice.
Barriers to entry (cost, licenses, brand) reduce competition.
Antitrust laws (Sherman Act 1890, Clayton Act 1914) protect competition.
fin: Banking is crowded: big national banks, community banks, credit unions and fintechs all compete for deposits and loans.
Many banks compete on non-price factors such as apps, service, branch access and no-fee accounts because their rates are similar.
Bank mergers are reviewed by regulators partly to make sure local competition survives.
ex: The U.S. had about 4,500 FDIC-insured banks at the end of 2024, plus thousands of credit unions (FDIC Quarterly Banking Profile; NCUA).
Online banks with no branches often pay much higher savings rates than the national average, forcing traditional banks to respond (FDIC national rates data).
Antitrust: in 2024 a federal judge ruled that Google illegally maintained a monopoly in online search (U.S. v. Google, D.D.C., Aug. 2024).
pis.trap: Don't say monopolistic competition is the same as a monopoly. Monopolistic competition has many sellers with slightly different products; a monopoly has one. Also, 'oligopoly' means few sellers, not necessarily that they cooperate (collusion is illegal).
pis.say: "Our client's bank can't win a rate war with online banks, so we'd compete on non-price factors: a local advisor, fast small-business loans and an easy app."

qs.q: How will our bank compete against online banks offering higher rates?
qs.a: We'd compete mainly on non-price factors, because matching rates would wipe out our margin. Online banks have low costs but no local relationships. We can offer what they can't: a local advisor, faster small-business loan decisions and in-person help. For example, community banks make a large share of small-business loans because they know local owners. So we'd keep rates competitive on one promotional CD and put our marketing behind service and relationships.

qs.q: Why do competitors in this market all charge similar prices?
qs.a: Because it's an oligopoly or close to one: a few big firms watch each other, so if one cuts price, the others match, and nobody gains. That's why they compete on brand, service and features instead. Airlines and wireless carriers work the same way. For this business, it means a price cut probably won't win lasting share. A better plan is to differentiate with service the big players don't offer.

cards: Competing on price versus competing on quality, service, convenience, brand or features.
A bank with a great app but average rates uses non-price competition.
A market with a few large sellers who watch and react to each other.
Many sellers of similar but differentiated products.

pis.title: Private enterprise
plain: Private enterprise (free enterprise) is an economic system in which individuals and businesses, not government, own most resources and decide what to produce. It rests on several features: private property (the right to own and use property, including businesses and investments), the profit motive (the chance to earn a reward for taking risk), competition (rivals keep prices and quality in check), freedom of choice (people choose what to buy, sell, where to work and what business to start) and voluntary exchange.

Government's role in private enterprise is limited but real: it protects property rights through laws and courts, enforces contracts and keeps markets competitive. Risk is part of the system: owners can earn profits, but they can also lose what they invest.
key: Private property: people can own businesses, homes and investments.
Profit motive: the reward for taking risk.
Competition and freedom of choice.
Voluntary exchange: both sides trade because they expect to gain.
Government protects property and enforces contracts.
fin: Lending depends on property rights: a car title or a home deed lets a lender use the property as collateral.
Owning stock is owning private property: shareholders share in profits through dividends and price gains.
Contracts (loan agreements, insurance policies) only work because courts enforce them.
ex: Americans filed a record 5.5 million applications to start new businesses in 2023 (U.S. Census Bureau, Business Formation Statistics).
Collateral in action: a mortgage lender can foreclose if payments stop because the home is the secured property, which is why mortgage rates are lower than credit card rates.
Shared ownership: anyone can own a slice of hundreds of private companies through an S&P 500 index fund.
pis.trap: Don't describe private enterprise as 'no government.' Government protects property rights and enforces contracts, which private enterprise needs. And profit isn't guaranteed: the right to profit comes with the risk of loss.
pis.say: "In our private-enterprise system, our client can own part of America's biggest companies through an index fund and share in their profits. That's why investing is how ordinary people build wealth."

qs.q: Why should a young person consider owning part of a business through stocks?
qs.a: Because private enterprise lets anyone share in business profits, not just founders. When you own stock, you own a small piece of private property in a company and earn dividends and growth. The S&P 500 has averaged roughly 10% a year since 1928, with ups and downs. Starting with even $50 a month in an index fund at 18 gives decades of compounding, which is the most powerful advantage a young investor has.

qs.q: What does the profit motive mean for our client's new business?
qs.a: It means the reward for taking risk, and it should shape every decision. The profit motive pushes our client to price correctly, control costs and serve customers better than competitors. But profit isn't guaranteed: about one in five new businesses fail in the first year, according to BLS data. So we'd build a budget that reaches break-even, keep a cash reserve and track profit monthly, so the risk our client takes actually pays off.

cards: An economic system where individuals own resources and make business decisions for profit, with limited government.
The desire to earn a reward for taking business risk; it drives innovation and efficiency.
Profit is not guaranteed; loss is possible.
The right of individuals and businesses to own, use and sell property.
Makes collateral, and therefore lending, possible.

pis.title: Factors affecting a business's profit
plain: Profit is what remains after expenses are subtracted from revenue: profit = revenue - expenses. Anything that changes revenue or expenses changes profit. Revenue depends on price and sales volume, which depend on demand, competition, marketing and the economy. Expenses include fixed costs (rent, insurance, salaries) and variable costs (materials, shipping, credit card processing fees).

Outside factors that affect profit include the economy (recessions lower sales), inflation (raises costs), interest rates (raise borrowing costs), competition (limits pricing power), government (taxes, regulations, tariffs) and technology. Inside factors include management decisions, efficiency, pricing strategy and the product mix. Profit margin, profit as a percentage of revenue, shows how much of each sales dollar the business keeps.
key: Profit = revenue - expenses.
Revenue = price × quantity sold.
Fixed vs variable costs.
Outside factors: economy, competition, inflation, interest rates, government.
Profit margin = profit ÷ revenue.
fin: Lenders analyze profit margins and trends to decide whether a borrower can repay.
A bank's own profit depends heavily on net interest margin: the gap between what it earns on loans and pays on deposits.
Advisors help small-business clients raise profit by cutting costs, adjusting prices or changing the product mix.
ex: Membership model: Costco earned about $4.8 billion in membership fees in fiscal 2024, a major share of its profit, letting it keep product markups low (Costco 2024 Annual Report).
Thin margins: grocery stores and restaurants often keep only a few cents of profit per dollar of sales, so a small cost increase can erase profit.
Tariffs and profit: import taxes raise costs for businesses that buy foreign goods; the average effective U.S. tariff rate was about 6.7% in July 2026 (Penn Wharton Budget Model, Sept. 2026).
pis.trap: Don't confuse revenue with profit. A business can grow sales and still lose money if costs grow faster. And cutting price doesn't always raise profit: it only helps if volume rises enough to make up for the lower margin.
pis.say: "Sales are up 20%, but profit fell because ingredient costs rose faster. Our plan targets margin, not just sales: renegotiate with suppliers and drop the two lowest-margin menu items."

qs.q: How can this business raise profit without raising prices?
qs.a: By cutting costs or selling more of its highest-margin products. Profit is revenue minus expenses, so lowering expenses works just as well as raising price. For example, the owner could renegotiate supplier contracts, cut waste and push the items with the best margins, like a coffee shop promoting drinks over food. We'd also look at the product mix: drop the lowest-margin items and train staff to upsell. That raises profit while keeping prices competitive.

qs.q: Why is a business with growing sales still losing money?
qs.a: Because expenses are growing faster than revenue. Sales are only half the profit equation. Rising ingredient costs, a new lease or discounts used to win sales can all eat the gain. Low prices can win volume while losing money on every unit. So we'd calculate the profit margin on each product, find which ones lose money and fix pricing or costs there first, before spending more to grow sales.

cards: A business can grow sales and still lose money.
Profit as a percentage of revenue: profit ÷ revenue.
Fixed costs stay the same at any sales level (rent); variable costs rise with sales (materials).

pis.title: Factors affecting business risk
plain: Business risk is the possibility of loss or failure. Risks are often grouped by cause. Economic risks come from changes in the economy: recessions, inflation, interest rates, competition and changes in demand. Natural risks come from nature: storms, floods, fires and pandemics. Human risks come from people: employee mistakes, theft, fraud, lawsuits and customer behavior. Businesses also face technological, legal/regulatory and political risks.

Pure risk offers only loss or no loss (a fire), and can usually be insured. Speculative risk offers a chance of gain or loss (launching a new product), and usually can't be insured. Some risks are controllable (training staff), and others are not (a recession). Businesses manage risk four ways: avoid it, reduce it, transfer it (insurance, contracts) or retain it (self-insure).
key: Economic, natural and human risks (plus technology, legal, political).
Pure risk (insurable) vs speculative risk (not insurable).
Controllable vs uncontrollable risk.
Manage risk: avoid, reduce, transfer, retain.
Concentration (relying on one customer, product or supplier) raises risk.
fin: Banks face credit risk (borrowers don't repay), interest-rate risk (rates change the value of loans and bonds), liquidity risk (depositors withdraw at once) and operational risk (fraud, outages).
Lenders price business loans by risk and require collateral or guarantees.
Insurance transfers pure risks such as property damage and liability.
ex: Interest-rate and liquidity risk: Silicon Valley Bank failed in March 2023 after customers tried to withdraw about $42 billion in a single day, following losses on bonds it bought when rates were low (FDIC; Federal Reserve review, 2023).
Technology risk: a faulty CrowdStrike software update in July 2024 crashed about 8.5 million Windows computers, grounding flights and disrupting banks (Microsoft; CrowdStrike, 2024).
Natural risk: a major hurricane can close a business for weeks; business interruption insurance replaces lost income during closure.
pis.trap: Don't say insurance can cover every risk. It covers pure risks (fire, theft, liability), not speculative ones like a product flopping or a competitor opening nearby. Those are managed through planning, diversification and cash reserves.
pis.say: "This business's biggest risk is concentration: 60% of sales come from one client. We'd reduce it by adding new customers, and transfer the pure risks like fire and liability with insurance."

qs.q: What is the biggest risk to this business, and how would you manage it?
qs.a: The biggest risk is usually the one that could close the business, so we'd look for concentration first: one big customer, one supplier or one product. Then we'd use the four methods: avoid, reduce, transfer or retain. For example, if 60% of sales come from one client, we reduce the risk by winning new customers, and we transfer pure risks like fire and liability through insurance. That way, one bad event can't sink our client's business.

qs.q: How would a recession affect this business?
qs.a: It depends on whether customers see the product as a need or a want. In a recession, unemployment rises and households cut discretionary spending first, so a restaurant or salon would see sales drop, while a grocery store stays steadier. Lenders also tighten credit. So we'd build a cash reserve of three to six months of fixed costs, keep a line of credit open before it's needed and identify which costs could be cut quickly if sales fell.

cards: Pure risk: only loss or no loss (insurable). Speculative risk: possible gain or loss (not insurable).
Fire = pure; new product launch = speculative.
Risks caused by changes in the economy, by nature, or by people.

pis.title: Small business and entrepreneurship in market economies
plain: Entrepreneurs start businesses by spotting needs and taking risks to meet them. Small businesses matter far beyond their size: they create jobs, introduce new products and services, increase competition that keeps big companies efficient, serve niche markets big firms ignore, and give people a path to building wealth. Many of today's largest companies started small.

Small businesses also face higher risk. They often lack access to capital, depend on the owner's skills and have little cushion when sales fall. That is why lenders, the Small Business Administration (SBA) and community banks play a big role in funding them.
key: Small businesses make up nearly all U.S. businesses and employ almost half of private workers.
They drive innovation and competition.
Entrepreneurs combine resources and take risk for profit.
Access to capital is the biggest challenge.
Government supports small business through the SBA.
fin: Community banks and credit unions are major lenders to local small businesses.
SBA loan guarantees reduce a bank's risk, so it can lend to businesses that wouldn't qualify otherwise.
Small-business owners need personal and business finance help: separating accounts, retirement plans (SEP-IRA, Solo 401(k)) and insurance.
ex: The U.S. had about 36.2 million small businesses, 99.9% of all businesses, employing about 62.3 million people, or 45.9% of U.S. employees (SBA Office of Advocacy, 2025 Small Business Profile).
Americans filed a record 5.5 million new business applications in 2023 (U.S. Census Bureau, Business Formation Statistics).
SBA 7(a) loans, the agency's main program, go up to $5 million with a government guarantee to the lender (SBA).
pis.trap: Don't say small businesses are 'less important' because each one is small. Together they employ almost half of private-sector workers. And entrepreneurship isn't only startups: buying a franchise or taking over a family business counts too.
pis.say: "Small businesses are 99.9% of U.S. businesses and employ about 46% of workers, according to the SBA. Lending to this owner isn't charity; it's how our bank grows with the local economy."

qs.q: Why should our bank make loans to small businesses?
qs.a: Because small businesses are the backbone of our local market and a profitable relationship for the bank. The SBA counts 36.2 million small businesses employing almost half of U.S. workers. When we lend to a local owner, we also win their deposits, payroll account and the owner's personal banking. SBA guarantees reduce our risk on loans that might not qualify otherwise. So a small-business loan program grows our customer base and supports the community at the same time.

qs.q: What role does a small business like this play in the local economy?
qs.a: A big one: it creates jobs, keeps money circulating locally and adds competition. A local bakery hires neighbors, buys from local suppliers and pays local taxes, and every dollar it earns gets spent again nearby. It also pushes bigger chains to keep prices and quality in check. That's why we'd help this owner grow carefully, with a loan sized to cash flow, so the business stays healthy and keeps those benefits in the community.

cards: A person who starts and runs a business, taking on risk in the hope of profit.
Entrepreneurship is one of the four factors of production.
Small businesses create jobs, add competition, drive innovation and serve niche markets.
The Small Business Administration guarantees part of a bank loan, reducing the lender's risk.

pis.title: The relationship between government and business
plain: Government and business depend on each other. Government plays several roles: regulator (setting rules for safety, fairness and the environment), protector (of consumers, workers, investors and competition), provider (of infrastructure, education, courts and public goods), purchaser (buying goods and services from businesses), taxer (raising revenue) and promoter (helping businesses through loans, grants, trade programs and research). Business in turn provides jobs, taxes and products, and influences government through lobbying and trade groups.

Finance is one of the most regulated industries. Major regulators include the Federal Reserve, the FDIC, the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC), the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB), the SEC and FINRA (a self-regulatory organization for brokers). Big laws such as the Dodd-Frank Act of 2010 followed the 2008 financial crisis.
key: Roles of government: regulate, protect, provide, purchase, tax, promote.
Antitrust laws protect competition.
Business influences government through lobbying and trade associations.
Regulation has costs (compliance) and benefits (trust, stability).
Finance regulators: Fed, FDIC, OCC, CFPB, SEC, FINRA.
fin: Deposit insurance (FDIC) is a government protection that makes people willing to keep money in banks.
Compliance costs are part of every bank's budget: anti-money-laundering checks, privacy rules and lending laws.
Government also promotes: SBA guarantees, export financing and tax incentives.
ex: Promoter role: the CHIPS and Science Act of 2022 provided about $52.7 billion to boost U.S. semiconductor manufacturing and research (U.S. Department of Commerce).
Protector role: the FDIC has insured deposits since 1933; no depositor has lost a penny of insured funds (FDIC).

Trade policy: on Feb. 20, 2026 the Supreme Court ruled 6-3 that the president could not use the International Emergency Economic Powers Act to impose tariffs, while tariffs under other trade laws stayed in place (Learning Resources v. Trump, 2026).
pis.trap: Don't paint regulation as only a burden. Rules like deposit insurance and disclosure requirements create the trust that lets finance work. The better answer weighs costs against benefits.
pis.say: "Government is both a rule maker and a partner. Rules like FDIC insurance build trust in banks, and programs like SBA guarantees make it possible for us to lend to this small business."

qs.q: Is government regulation good or bad for banks?
qs.a: Both, and the balance matters. Regulation adds compliance costs and limits some activities, but it also creates the trust banking depends on. FDIC insurance is the best example: since 1933, no depositor has lost insured money, so people are willing to keep their savings in banks. After 2008, stronger capital rules made banks safer. So for our client's bank, the goal isn't to fight regulation but to comply efficiently and use the trust it creates as a selling point.

qs.q: How could a government program help this business?
qs.a: Government acts as a promoter, not just a regulator. This business could use an SBA-guaranteed loan, which lowers the bank's risk so the owner can borrow with a smaller down payment. Local governments offer grants, tax credits or training programs, and the Export-Import Bank helps with overseas sales. We'd check SBA, state and local programs first, because cheaper capital lowers the business's costs and helps it grow faster.

cards: Regulator, protector, provider, purchaser, taxer and promoter.
Laws that protect competition by banning monopolies and unfair practices.
Financial reform law passed after the 2008 crisis; created the CFPB and tightened bank rules.

pis.title: The nature of taxes
plain: Taxes are required payments to government that fund public services such as roads, schools, defense and Social Security. Major types include income taxes (on earnings), payroll taxes (Social Security and Medicare, withheld from paychecks), sales taxes (on purchases), property taxes (on real estate), excise taxes (on specific goods like gasoline and tobacco), corporate income taxes and tariffs (taxes on imports).

Tax structures describe who bears the burden. A progressive tax takes a larger percentage from higher incomes (the federal income tax, with rates from 10% to 37%). A proportional (flat) tax takes the same percentage from everyone (the 21% federal corporate rate). A regressive tax takes a larger share of income from lower earners, even if the rate is the same (sales taxes, because lower-income households spend more of their income). Taxes also shape behavior: tax-advantaged accounts like 401(k)s and Roth IRAs encourage saving.
key: Purpose: fund government and shape behavior.
Types: income, payroll, sales, property, excise, corporate, tariffs.
Progressive, proportional and regressive structures.
Employees pay 7.65% in payroll taxes (6.2% Social Security + 1.45% Medicare).
Tax-advantaged accounts encourage saving.
fin: Advisors plan around taxes: Roth vs traditional, tax-loss harvesting and choosing tax-advantaged accounts first.
Business owners pay self-employment tax of 15.3% on net earnings because they pay both halves of payroll taxes.
Where a business locates affects its tax bill: state income, sales and property taxes vary widely.
ex: The federal corporate income tax rate has been a flat 21% since 2018 (Tax Cuts and Jobs Act).
Five states have no statewide sales tax: Alaska, Delaware, Montana, New Hampshire and Oregon (state revenue departments), and states such as Texas and Florida have no state income tax on wages.
For 2027 the standard deduction rises to $16,600 for single filers, and the seven federal rates (10% to 37%) stay the same (IRS Rev. Proc. 2026-35).
pis.trap: Don't say a sales tax is progressive because rich people buy more. It's regressive because it takes a bigger share of a lower-income household's income. Also, moving into a higher bracket only taxes the dollars above the threshold at the higher rate.
pis.say: "Because the income tax is progressive, a raise only taxes the extra dollars at the higher rate. Our client will always take home more after a raise."

qs.q: How do taxes affect where this business should locate?
qs.a: Taxes are a cost, so they directly affect profit, but they're only one factor. States differ in income, sales and property taxes: Texas and Florida have no state income tax on wages, while five states have no statewide sales tax. A lower-tax location can cut costs, but if it's far from customers or skilled workers, sales suffer. So we'd compare the full cost, taxes plus rent, wages and access to customers, before recommending a location.

qs.q: Is a sales tax fair to lower-income customers?
qs.a: Economists call sales taxes regressive, because lower-income households spend more of their income, so the tax takes a bigger share of what they earn. Someone earning $30,000 who spends it all pays a much larger share than someone earning $300,000 who saves a lot. That's why many states exempt groceries or medicine. For our client, it means budgets should include sales tax on big purchases, and lower-income households should plan for it.

cards: A tax that takes a higher percentage of income as income rises.
A tax that takes a larger share of income from lower earners.
A tax that takes the same percentage from everyone.

pis.title: Organized labor and business
plain: Organized labor means workers joining together in labor unions to bargain with employers as a group. Through collective bargaining, a union negotiates wages, benefits, hours, safety rules and job security in a contract. If talks fail, workers may strike (stop working), and employers may lock out workers. Mediation and arbitration are ways to settle disputes with a neutral third party.

The National Labor Relations Act of 1935 (Wagner Act) gave most private-sector workers the right to organize and bargain; the Taft-Hartley Act of 1947 limited some union practices and let states pass right-to-work laws, which bar contracts that require workers to pay union fees. Unions can raise pay and benefits and give workers a voice, but they can also raise labor costs and make it harder for businesses to change quickly.
key: Unions bargain collectively for wages, benefits and working conditions.
Tools: strikes (workers), lockouts (employers), mediation, arbitration.
NLRA (1935) protects the right to organize; Taft-Hartley (1947) allowed right-to-work laws.
Union membership is much higher in the public sector than the private sector.
Union contracts affect a company's costs, flexibility and risk.
fin: Lenders and investors look at labor contracts because they lock in costs for years.
Strikes are an operating risk: lost production can hurt sales, profits and loan repayment.
Union pension and benefit plans are major institutional investors.
ex: Union membership was 10.0% of U.S. wage and salary workers in 2025: 32.9% in the public sector versus 5.9% in the private sector (BLS, released Feb. 18, 2026).
The 2023 United Auto Workers strike against Ford, GM and Stellantis ended with contracts raising base wages by about 25% over the life of the deal (UAW; company statements, 2023).
Michigan repealed its right-to-work law effective in 2024, leaving 26 right-to-work states (Michigan Legislature; National Conference of State Legislatures).
pis.trap: Don't say unions only hurt business. They raise costs, but they can also lower turnover, improve training and make labor costs predictable for years. A balanced answer names both sides.
pis.say: "A union contract locks in labor costs for four years. For our loan analysis that's actually helpful: we know the wage increases in advance and can build them into the cash flow plan."

qs.q: How would a union contract affect this company's costs and its loan?
qs.a: It would make labor costs higher but more predictable. A contract sets wages and benefits for several years, like the 2023 UAW deals that raised base pay about 25% over the contract. For a lender, predictability helps: we can build every scheduled raise into the cash flow forecast. The risk is a strike when the contract expires, so we'd check the expiration date, make sure the company holds cash reserves and size the loan payment to the higher labor costs.

qs.q: Should a business owner worry if employees want to unionize?
qs.a: The owner should listen, not panic, and must not interfere, because workers have a legal right to organize under the National Labor Relations Act. A union push usually signals concerns about pay, schedules or respect. Addressing those directly, with fair pay and open communication, often matters more than the vote itself. If employees do unionize, a good contract can reduce turnover. So we'd advise the owner to review pay and benefits against the market and talk with employees openly.

cards: Negotiation between a union and an employer over wages, benefits and working conditions.
A state law that bans contracts requiring workers to pay union fees as a condition of employment.
A strike is workers stopping work; a lockout is an employer keeping workers out.
Mediation and arbitration can settle disputes.

pis.title: Productivity
plain: Productivity measures how efficiently inputs are turned into outputs: output divided by input. Labor productivity, the most common measure, is output per hour worked. A business becomes more productive when it produces more with the same resources, or the same amount with fewer.

Productivity rises through better technology and equipment (capital), education and training (human capital), better processes and management, and specialization. It matters because, over time, productivity growth is the main source of higher wages, profits and living standards. When productivity grows faster than wages, unit labor costs fall, which helps businesses hold prices down.
key: Productivity = output ÷ input.
Labor productivity = output per hour worked.
Raised by technology, training, better processes, specialization.
Higher productivity supports higher wages and lower costs.
Unit labor costs fall when productivity grows faster than pay.
fin: Banks raise productivity with automation: mobile deposit, online account opening and AI-assisted fraud detection let fewer staff serve more customers.
Lenders like productivity investments because equipment that raises output can pay for itself.
Advisors use planning software and client portals to serve more households per advisor.
ex: U.S. nonfarm business productivity rose at a 3.6% annual rate in the third quarter of 2026 and 2.1% over the previous year, while unit labor costs fell 0.7% (BLS preliminary release, Nov. 5, 2026).
Automation in finance: mobile check deposit and online account opening let customers do in minutes what once required a teller.
Training pays: better-trained workers make fewer errors and serve more customers per hour.
pis.trap: Don't confuse productivity with production. Production is the total amount made; productivity is how much is made per unit of input. A business can produce more just by hiring more people while its productivity stays the same or falls.
pis.say: "This equipment loan raises productivity: the same three employees can serve 40% more customers. That extra output is what repays the loan."

qs.q: How could this business get more done without hiring?
qs.a: By raising productivity: more output from the same workers and hours. The main levers are technology, training and better processes. For example, an online booking system cuts phone time, a second oven doubles baking capacity, and cross-training staff covers busy hours without new hires. U.S. productivity grew 3.6% at an annual rate in the third quarter of 2026, largely from businesses doing just this. We'd finance the equipment with a loan the extra sales can repay.

qs.q: Why does productivity matter for the whole economy?
qs.a: Because over the long run, productivity is what raises living standards. When workers produce more per hour, businesses can pay higher wages without raising prices, and profits can grow too. In the third quarter of 2026, U.S. productivity rose 3.6% at an annual rate while unit labor costs fell 0.7%, which eases inflation pressure. For our client, a more productive economy means stronger company earnings over time, which supports long-term investing.

cards: Output per unit of input; how efficiently resources are used.
Labor productivity = output per hour worked.
Production is the total output; productivity is output per unit of input.
Hiring more can raise production without raising productivity.
Labor cost per unit of output; falls when productivity grows faster than wages.

pis.title: Specialization and division of labor
plain: Specialization means focusing on a limited set of tasks or products. Division of labor breaks a job into smaller steps, with each worker doing one step. Both raise productivity: workers get faster and more skilled through repetition, less time is lost switching tasks, and specialized tools can be used.

Adam Smith described this in The Wealth of Nations (1776) with a pin factory where ten workers, each doing one step, could make about 48,000 pins a day, far more than they could alone. Henry Ford's moving assembly line in 1913 cut the time to build a Model T from about 12 hours to about 90 minutes. Specialization also has downsides: boring, repetitive work, workers who can't do other tasks, and dependence on every step running smoothly. Countries specialize too, producing what they make most efficiently and trading for the rest.
key: Specialization: focusing on fewer tasks or products.
Division of labor: dividing a job into steps done by different workers.
Raises productivity through skill, speed and less switching time.
Downsides: boredom, narrow skills, interdependence.
Specialization requires trade (and money) to get everything else.
fin: Banks divide labor: tellers, loan officers, underwriters, compliance officers and advisors each handle a part of the customer relationship.
Financial planners specialize (retirement, tax, estate) and refer clients to each other.
Specialization is why money matters: people trade what they specialize in for everything else.
ex: Smith's pin factory: ten workers dividing the steps could make about 48,000 pins a day (Adam Smith, The Wealth of Nations, 1776).
Ford's moving assembly line (1913) cut Model T assembly time from about 12 hours to about 90 minutes (Ford Motor Company history).
In a mortgage process, an underwriter who reviews loans all day spots risks faster than a generalist.
pis.trap: Don't present specialization as all upside. Too much specialization means workers can't cover for each other and one bottleneck stops everything. The best answer recommends specializing core tasks while cross-training for backup.
pis.say: "Right now the owner does everything. If the owner focuses on sales and the bookkeeper handles the accounts, each one gets faster at their part, which is division of labor in action."

qs.q: Should the owner keep doing everything personally?
qs.a: No. Specialization would make the business more productive. When the owner handles bookkeeping, ordering and sales alone, time is lost switching tasks and no area gets full attention. Adam Smith's pin factory showed how dividing steps multiplies output. So we'd recommend the owner focus on what drives revenue, like sales and customer relationships, and hand bookkeeping to a part-time accountant or software. The hours freed up are worth more than the cost.

qs.q: What are the downsides of specializing too much?
qs.a: Work can become repetitive, workers lose flexibility and the business depends on every specialist showing up. If only one person knows payroll and they leave, the business is stuck. Factories with strict division of labor also see boredom and turnover. So we'd specialize the core roles but cross-train each employee on at least one backup task. That keeps the productivity gains while protecting the business when someone is out.

cards: Breaking a job into separate steps, each done by a different worker.
Smith's pin factory, Ford's assembly line.
Focusing on a limited number of tasks or products to become more efficient.
Repetitive work, narrow skills and dependence on every step running smoothly.

pis.title: The law of diminishing returns
plain: The law of diminishing returns says that if you keep adding more of one input, like workers, while other inputs stay fixed, like space and equipment, each additional unit eventually adds less output than the one before. The extra output from one more unit of input is called the marginal product.

Picture a small bakery with one oven. The second worker adds a lot of output, because tasks can be divided. The third adds a bit less. By the fifth, workers are waiting for the oven and getting in each other's way, so extra output is tiny or even negative. The fix is not more workers but more of the fixed input: a second oven or a bigger kitchen. The law applies in the short run, when at least one input can't change.
key: Adding more of one input to fixed inputs eventually adds less output each time.
Marginal product = extra output from one more unit of input.
Applies in the short run, when some inputs are fixed.
Diminishing returns does not mean output falls, only that gains get smaller (at first).
Solution: expand the fixed input (equipment, space).
fin: Lenders check whether a loan request expands the bottleneck input (a second oven) or just adds more of the input already in surplus.
Marketing budgets show diminishing returns: each extra $1,000 in ads brings fewer new customers.
Banks see diminishing returns from adding branches in a market they already cover.
ex: Bakery math: one oven, one worker makes 100 loaves; two workers 180; three 230; four 250. The fourth worker adds only 20 loaves, a sign to buy another oven instead of hiring.
Studying works the same way: the fifth straight hour of cramming adds less than the first hour.
Farming: adding more fertilizer to the same field raises yields at first, then barely at all.
pis.trap: Don't confuse diminishing returns with negative returns. Diminishing returns means each extra worker adds less; negative returns means an extra worker actually lowers total output. Also, it isn't the same as economies of scale, which is about growing all inputs together in the long run.
pis.say: "The fourth worker added only 20 loaves, compared with 80 from the second. That's diminishing returns: the oven is the bottleneck. Instead of hiring, we'd finance a second oven."

qs.q: Should the bakery hire a fourth worker?
qs.a: Probably not yet, because of diminishing returns. With one oven fixed, each new worker adds less: if the second worker added 80 loaves and the fourth adds only 20, the oven is the bottleneck. A fourth worker costs the same wage but produces a fraction of the output. So we'd compare the marginal revenue from those 20 loaves with the wage. If it doesn't cover the cost, a better move is financing a second oven, which lets every worker produce more.

qs.q: Why might opening more branches stop paying off?
qs.a: Because of diminishing returns: each additional branch in the same area adds fewer new customers than the last, since the market is already covered and branches start competing with each other. More customers now bank on their phones, too. So instead of a sixth branch, we'd put that money into the mobile app and a small-business lending team, which reach new customers the branches can't.

cards: Adding more of one input to fixed inputs eventually adds less output per unit.
The fifth worker sharing one oven adds little.
The extra output from adding one more unit of an input.
Falls as diminishing returns set in.
An input that can't be changed in the short run, such as equipment or space.

pis.title: Gross Domestic Product (GDP)
plain: Gross Domestic Product (GDP) is the total market value of all final goods and services produced within a country's borders in a period, usually a quarter or a year. It is the broadest measure of the size and health of an economy. Using the expenditure approach, GDP = C + I + G + (X - M): consumer spending, business investment, government purchases and net exports (exports minus imports).

Nominal GDP uses current prices; real GDP adjusts for inflation, so it shows whether the economy actually produced more. GDP per capita divides GDP by population to compare living standards. In the U.S., the Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA) publishes GDP every quarter as an annualized growth rate, first as an advance estimate and later revised. GDP has limits: it leaves out unpaid work like caring for family, the underground economy, and measures of well-being such as leisure or the environment.
key: GDP = market value of all final goods and services produced in a country.
GDP = C + I + G + (X - M).
Real GDP removes inflation; nominal doesn't.
GDP per capita compares living standards.
Only final goods count, to avoid double counting.
fin: Rising real GDP usually means rising company earnings, more hiring and fewer loan defaults.
Banks use GDP forecasts to plan lending and set aside reserves for losses.
Investors compare GDP growth across countries when deciding where to invest.
ex: Real GDP grew at a 3.4% annual rate in the third quarter of 2026, up from 2.2% in the second quarter (BEA advance estimate, Oct. 29, 2026).
U.S. nominal GDP was about $29 trillion in 2024, the largest in the world (BEA; IMF World Economic Outlook).
Consumer spending makes up about 68% of U.S. GDP, by far the biggest component (BEA).
pis.trap: Don't count intermediate goods. The flour a bakery buys is already inside the price of the bread, so counting both would double count. And don't compare nominal GDP across years without adjusting for inflation.
pis.say: "Real GDP grew at a 3.4% annual rate last quarter, so the economy is still expanding. That supports our client's plan to expand, but we'd still keep a cash cushion in case growth slows."

qs.q: What does GDP growth tell our client about the economy?
qs.a: It tells us whether the economy is producing more, which drives jobs, wages and company profits. Real GDP grew at a 3.4% annual rate in the third quarter of 2026, which means the economy is expanding, not in recession. For our client, an expanding economy is a reasonable time to invest steadily and keep their job secure. But GDP looks backward, so we'd still build a three-to-six-month emergency fund in case growth slows.

qs.q: Why does a bank care about GDP?
qs.a: Because GDP growth drives loan demand and loan quality. When the economy grows, businesses borrow to expand and borrowers repay on time; when GDP shrinks, defaults rise. Since consumer spending is about 68% of GDP, a slowdown hits a bank's card and auto loans first. So a bank watches GDP to decide how fast to grow lending and how much to set aside for losses, which protects depositors and shareholders.

cards: The total market value of all final goods and services produced within a country in a period.
Real GDP is adjusted for inflation; nominal GDP uses current prices.
Use real GDP to tell if output actually grew.
GDP divided by population; a rough measure of living standards.
Lets you compare countries of different sizes.

pis.title: Consumer spending as an economic indicator
plain: Consumer spending is what households spend on goods and services, from groceries to rent to haircuts. In the U.S. it makes up about 68% of GDP, so it is the single biggest driver of the economy. When households spend more, businesses sell more, hire more and invest more; when households pull back, the slowdown spreads.

Economists track it several ways. Personal consumption expenditures (PCE), from the BEA each month, measure total spending. Retail sales, from the Census Bureau, measure store and online sales and come out sooner. Surveys of consumer sentiment (University of Michigan) and consumer confidence (The Conference Board) measure how people feel, which can hint at future spending. The personal saving rate shows how much of after-tax income households save instead of spend.
key: Consumer spending is about 68% of U.S. GDP.
Measured by PCE (BEA) and retail sales (Census).
Sentiment and confidence surveys measure attitudes, which may predict spending.
The saving rate shows the cushion households have.
Real spending (inflation-adjusted) matters more than nominal.
fin: Card issuers and banks see spending in real time through transaction data and watch for rising delinquencies.
Retail and restaurant borrowers depend on consumer spending, so lenders watch it when underwriting.
A low saving rate means households have less cushion if layoffs rise.
ex: In September 2026, consumer spending (PCE) rose 0.5%, but after inflation real spending was nearly flat (less than 0.1%), and the personal saving rate was 3.8% (BEA, Oct. 29, 2026).

The University of Michigan's consumer sentiment index rose to a preliminary 51.0 in November 2026 from 48.0 in October, after a record low of 44.8 in May 2026 (University of Michigan Surveys of Consumers, Nov. 2026).
Consumer spending is about 68% of GDP (BEA).
pis.trap: Don't treat a rise in nominal spending as good news by itself. If prices rose as much as spending, people bought the same amount or less. Also, sentiment and spending don't always move together: people can feel gloomy and keep spending.
pis.say: "Spending rose 0.5% in September, but after inflation it was nearly flat. That tells us families are paying more for the same things, which is why we'd keep this retailer's inventory lean."

qs.q: Consumers say they feel gloomy but keep spending. Which should a business believe?
qs.a: Watch what people do more than what they say, but don't ignore the mood. Spending is the real data; sentiment is an early warning. In 2026, sentiment hit a record low of 44.8 in May while spending kept growing, but by September real spending was nearly flat and the saving rate was just 3.8%. That combination says households are stretched. So we'd tell this business to plan for slower sales: keep inventory lean and avoid big fixed commitments until spending picks up.

qs.q: What would falling consumer spending mean for this retailer's loan?
qs.a: It would raise the risk that the retailer can't make payments, because about 68% of the economy is consumer spending and retailers feel a slowdown first. Lower sales with the same rent and payroll squeezes cash flow. So we'd stress-test the loan: could the business still pay if sales fell 15%? We'd also add a cash-reserve requirement and a line of credit so a slow season doesn't turn into a missed payment.

cards: The BEA's monthly measure of total household spending on goods and services.
A survey measure of how consumers feel about their finances and the economy.
University of Michigan index: 51.0 prelim, Nov. 2026.
The share of after-tax income households save.

pis.title: Unemployment rates
plain: The unemployment rate is the percentage of the labor force that is jobless but actively looking for work. The labor force includes people who are working or looking; people who aren't looking, like retirees and full-time students, aren't counted. The Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) publishes the rate monthly in the Employment Situation report, along with how many jobs employers added.

There are four main types of unemployment: frictional (between jobs or just entering the workforce), structural (skills don't match available jobs, often because of technology or industry change), cyclical (caused by a recession) and seasonal (jobs that disappear at certain times of year). Even a healthy economy has some unemployment. High unemployment means lost income, lower spending, lower tax revenue and more loan defaults. Very low unemployment can push wages up and make hiring hard for businesses.
key: Unemployment rate = unemployed ÷ labor force.
To be unemployed you must be looking for work.
Types: frictional, structural, cyclical, seasonal.
Reported monthly by the BLS.
Unemployment is a lagging indicator: it often rises after a recession starts.
fin: Job loss is the biggest cause of missed loan payments, which is why advisors stress emergency funds.
Banks raise loan-loss reserves when unemployment is expected to climb.
Low unemployment gives workers bargaining power, raising wages and business costs.
ex: The unemployment rate was 4.1% in October 2026, as employers added 165,000 jobs (BLS Employment Situation, Nov. 2026).
Unemployment hit 14.8% in April 2020, the highest since the BLS began tracking in 1948, then fell quickly as the economy reopened (BLS).
Structural change: as banks moved to mobile apps, demand for tellers fell while demand for software and cybersecurity staff grew (BLS Occupational Outlook Handbook).
pis.trap: Don't say everyone without a job is unemployed. Retirees, full-time students and people who stopped looking are outside the labor force. Also, 'full employment' doesn't mean 0% unemployment, because frictional unemployment always exists.
pis.say: "Unemployment is 4.1%, so jobs are fairly plentiful, but layoffs can hit any industry. That's why step one for our client is three to six months of expenses in a high-yield savings account."

qs.q: If our client lost their job tomorrow, what would protect them?
qs.a: An emergency fund first, then insurance and a plan. Job loss is the most common reason people fall behind on bills, so we'd build three to six months of expenses in a high-yield savings account. State unemployment benefits replace only part of pay for a limited time. Even with unemployment at 4.1% in October 2026, layoffs happen in every industry. So we'd automate savings now, keep credit card balances low and update the resume, so a layoff becomes a setback instead of a crisis.

qs.q: Why does a low unemployment rate make it hard for this business to hire?
qs.a: Because when most people who want jobs already have one, employers compete for fewer available workers, which pushes wages up. With unemployment around 4%, this business is bidding against bigger firms. So we'd recommend competing on more than pay: flexible schedules, training and a clear path to promotion, plus a referral bonus. Raising productivity with better equipment also means the business needs fewer new hires to grow.

cards: The percentage of the labor force that is jobless and actively looking for work.
Frictional (between jobs), structural (skills mismatch), cyclical (recession), seasonal.
People 16 and older who are working or actively looking for work.
Retirees and full-time students aren't in it.

pis.title: The economic impact of inflation on business
plain: Inflation is a general rise in prices over time, which means each dollar buys less. In the U.S. it is measured mainly by the Consumer Price Index (CPI) from the BLS and the PCE price index from the BEA; the Federal Reserve targets 2% inflation, measured by PCE. Demand-pull inflation happens when spending grows faster than the economy can produce; cost-push inflation happens when costs like energy or wages rise.

For businesses, inflation raises the cost of materials, energy, rent and wages. Owners must decide whether to raise prices and risk losing customers or absorb costs and accept lower margins. Inflation makes planning harder, because future costs are uncertain, and it usually leads to higher interest rates as the Fed responds, raising borrowing costs. Some effects help: borrowers with fixed-rate debt repay with dollars worth less, and inventory bought earlier can be sold at higher prices. Cash sitting idle loses buying power.
key: Inflation = general rise in prices; purchasing power falls.
Measured by CPI (BLS) and PCE price index (BEA); Fed target 2%.
Demand-pull vs cost-push.
Business impact: higher costs, pricing decisions, wage pressure, higher rates.
Fixed-rate borrowers benefit; savers in cash lose.
fin: Lenders raise rates when inflation rises, so variable-rate business loans get more expensive.
Advisors move idle cash into high-yield savings, Treasury bills or I bonds so it keeps up with inflation.
Businesses review contracts: escalation clauses let prices rise with costs.
ex: Consumer prices rose 3.7% in the 12 months through September 2026, above the Fed's 2% target; the PCE price index rose 3.6% (BLS; BEA, Oct. 2026).
