Cost-push example: gasoline topped $4.50 a gallon in spring 2026 amid shipping disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz, raising delivery and travel costs for businesses (BLS CPI releases; University of Michigan, 2026).
CPI inflation peaked at 9.1% in June 2022, the highest in about 40 years (BLS).
pis.trap: Don't say inflation means 'prices are high.' It means prices are rising. If inflation falls from 4% to 3%, prices are still going up, just more slowly (that's disinflation; deflation is falling prices). And inflation doesn't hurt everyone equally: fixed-rate borrowers can gain.
pis.say: "With inflation at 3.7%, the owner's costs are rising every month. Rather than a big price increase that scares customers off, we'd raise prices a little on the highest-demand items and lock in a fixed-rate loan now."

qs.q: Should this business raise prices because of inflation?
qs.a: Probably yes, but carefully and selectively. With inflation at 3.7% in September 2026, the owner's costs are rising, and absorbing all of it shrinks margins. The key is demand: raise prices most on items customers value most and have few substitutes for, and less on price-sensitive items. Small, regular increases tend to cause less pushback than one big jump. We'd also cut waste and renegotiate with suppliers, so the business protects its margin without losing loyal customers.

qs.q: How does inflation hurt a small business that has cash sitting in the bank?
qs.a: Cash earning little or nothing loses buying power every year. At 3.7% inflation, $50,000 in a 0.5% account buys about $1,600 less in a year. The business still needs some cash for operations and emergencies, but extra reserves should earn more. We'd move the reserve into a high-yield business savings account, a money market fund or short-term Treasury bills, keeping it safe and available while it keeps pace with rising costs.

cards: A general rise in prices over time, which lowers the purchasing power of money.
Demand-pull: spending grows faster than output. Cost-push: input costs like energy or wages rise.
A gas price spike causes cost-push inflation.
Disinflation: prices rise more slowly. Deflation: prices actually fall.
Inflation falling from 4% to 3% is disinflation.

pis.title: The economic impact of interest-rate fluctuations
plain: An interest rate is the price of borrowing money and the reward for saving it. The Federal Reserve sets a target range for the federal funds rate, the rate banks charge each other for overnight loans, and that ripples out to other rates. Many banks set their prime rate at the top of the Fed's range plus 3 percentage points, and credit cards, business lines of credit and home equity lines often float above prime. Longer-term rates, like 30-year mortgages, follow Treasury yields, which reflect expected inflation and growth.

When rates rise, borrowing costs more, so households buy fewer homes and cars, businesses delay expansion, and spending slows, which helps cool inflation. Savers earn more. Prices of existing bonds fall, and stock valuations often drop. A higher rate can also strengthen the dollar. When rates fall, the opposite happens: borrowing and spending pick up, savers earn less, and existing bonds rise in value.
key: Interest rate = price of borrowing, reward for saving.
The Fed sets the federal funds target range; other rates follow.
Prime rate usually = top of the Fed range + 3 points.
Higher rates: less borrowing and spending, more saving, lower bond prices, stronger dollar.
Fixed vs variable rates decide who feels the change.
fin: Variable-rate loans (credit cards, HELOCs, business lines of credit) reprice quickly when the Fed moves.
Banks earn the spread between loan rates and deposit rates; rate changes squeeze or widen that margin.
Advisors use rate cycles in advice: lock fixed rates when they're likely to rise, ladder CDs to balance yield and access.
ex: The Fed raised its target range by 0.25 point to 3.75%-4.00% on Sept. 16, 2026 and held it on Oct. 28, 2026; its next meeting is Dec. 8-9, 2026 (Federal Reserve).
That puts the prime rate at about 7.00% (the top of the Fed's range plus 3 points, the convention most banks use).
The average 30-year fixed mortgage rate was about 7.11% for the week of Nov. 12, 2026 (Freddie Mac).
pis.trap: Don't say the Fed sets mortgage or credit card rates directly. It sets the federal funds target; other rates respond, and long-term rates also depend on markets. And remember bond prices move opposite to rates.
pis.say: "The Fed raised rates to 3.75%-4.00% in September, so the owner's variable-rate line of credit now costs more. We'd move the long-term equipment balance into a fixed-rate term loan so future hikes can't raise the payment."

qs.q: Should this business borrow now or wait for rates to fall?
qs.a: Decide based on the project's return, not a rate forecast, because nobody can time rates reliably. If the new equipment earns more than the loan costs, waiting means losing that profit. With the prime rate around 7%, we'd borrow only what the project needs, choose a fixed rate so the payment can't rise, and make sure there's no prepayment penalty. If rates fall later, the business can refinance. That captures the opportunity now while limiting rate risk.

qs.q: How do rising rates help or hurt our client?
qs.a: It depends which side of the rate they're on. As a saver, our client earns more: high-yield savings and CDs pay more when the Fed raises rates. As a borrower, especially with variable-rate debt like credit cards, they pay more, since card rates move with prime. So we'd pay down the credit card balance first, since it's the most expensive debt, and lock some savings into a CD ladder to earn today's higher rates.

cards: The rate banks charge each other for overnight loans; the Fed sets a target range.
The base rate banks charge their best borrowers, usually the top of the Fed's range + 3 points.
When interest rates rise, prices of existing bonds fall, and vice versa.

pis.title: Business cycles
plain: The business cycle is the repeated rise and fall of economic activity over time. It has four phases. In an expansion, GDP grows, unemployment falls, and businesses hire and invest. At the peak, growth tops out, often with rising inflation. In a contraction, GDP falls, unemployment rises and spending slows; a deep, lasting contraction is a recession, and a severe one is a depression. At the trough, the economy bottoms out, then recovery begins and a new expansion starts.

In the U.S., the National Bureau of Economic Research (NBER) officially dates recessions, looking at many indicators, not just two quarters of falling GDP. Cycles vary in length: the 2020 recession lasted only two months, while the Great Recession lasted 18 months. Businesses respond differently in each phase, and industries differ: cyclical industries (cars, travel, home building, luxury goods) swing with the cycle, while defensive industries (groceries, utilities, health care) stay steadier.
key: Phases: expansion, peak, contraction (recession), trough, then recovery.
NBER officially dates U.S. recessions.
Cyclical industries swing hard; defensive industries stay steady.
Indicators: leading (stock prices, building permits), coincident (GDP, payrolls), lagging (unemployment).
Businesses expand in good times and protect cash in downturns.
fin: Lenders tighten credit near peaks and in contractions, so businesses should line up credit before they need it.
Advisors use the cycle to explain why diversified portfolios and emergency funds matter: downturns are normal, not rare.
Banks build loan-loss reserves ahead of expected downturns.
ex: The Great Recession lasted 18 months (December 2007 to June 2009); the 2020 recession lasted two months (February to April 2020), the shortest on record (NBER).
Today: real GDP grew at a 3.4% annual rate in Q3 2026 and unemployment was 4.1% in October, consistent with an expansion (BEA; BLS).
Defensive vs cyclical: grocery chains held up through 2008-09 while home builders and automakers cut deeply.
pis.trap: Don't define a recession only as 'two quarters of negative GDP.' That's a rule of thumb; the NBER uses a broader set of data. And don't promise when the next recession will come. Nobody can time the cycle reliably.
pis.say: "The economy is in an expansion now, with 3.4% GDP growth, but every expansion ends eventually. So we'd use the good times to build cash reserves and open a line of credit before this business needs it."

qs.q: How should this business prepare for the next recession?
qs.a: Prepare in the expansion, because banks lend most easily when times are good. First, build cash reserves of three to six months of fixed costs. Second, open a line of credit now, even if unused. Third, keep some costs flexible, like part-time staff or month-to-month contracts. In 2008-09, businesses with cash and credit lines survived while others closed. With GDP growing 3.4% in late 2026, now is the time to set this up, so a downturn becomes a challenge instead of a crisis.

qs.q: Which phase of the business cycle are we in right now, and why does it matter?
qs.a: The data point to an expansion: real GDP grew at a 3.4% annual rate in the third quarter of 2026 and unemployment was 4.1%. But inflation is 3.7% and the Fed raised rates in September, which are signs of a late-stage expansion. It matters because the right moves differ by phase. For this client, it means borrowing carefully at fixed rates, avoiding stretched expansion plans and building reserves now, while credit is still available.

cards: The repeated rise and fall of economic activity: expansion, peak, contraction, trough.
A significant, widespread decline in economic activity lasting more than a few months.
Cyclical industries swing with the economy; defensive industries stay steady.
Cars and travel vs groceries and utilities.

pis.title: The role of business in society
plain: Businesses exist to produce the goods and services people want, but their role in society is bigger than that. They create jobs and income, pay taxes that fund schools and roads, develop new products and technologies, create returns for investors and savers, and support communities through local spending and giving. In return, society expects businesses to obey laws, treat workers and customers fairly and limit harm to the environment.

Social responsibility is the idea that businesses have obligations to all stakeholders, not only owners. Stakeholders include customers, employees, suppliers, the community, government and shareholders. In 2019 the Business Roundtable, a group of major company CEOs, changed its statement on the purpose of a corporation to commit to all stakeholders rather than shareholders alone.
key: Business provides goods, services, jobs, income and taxes.
Businesses drive innovation and economic growth.
Stakeholders: customers, employees, suppliers, community, government, owners.
Social responsibility: obligations beyond profit.
Profit and responsibility can support each other.
fin: Banks channel savings into loans that build homes, businesses and communities.
The Community Reinvestment Act of 1977 requires banks to help meet the credit needs of the communities they serve, including low- and moderate-income neighborhoods.
Financial education programs build trust and future customers.
ex: The Community Reinvestment Act (1977) requires federally insured banks to serve the credit needs of their whole communities, and regulators rate how well they do (FDIC; OCC; Federal Reserve).
In 2019, the Business Roundtable's new 'Statement on the Purpose of a Corporation' committed member CEOs to customers, employees, suppliers, communities and shareholders (Business Roundtable).
Small businesses employ about 46% of U.S. workers (SBA Office of Advocacy, 2025).
pis.trap: Don't frame it as profit versus society. Profitable businesses create jobs and taxes, and responsible practices often build loyalty that raises profit. The strong answer shows how both work together.
pis.say: "A bank's role goes beyond earning interest. When we lend to local businesses and teach financial literacy, we create jobs and future customers, and the Community Reinvestment Act expects us to."

qs.q: Why should a bank care about the community and not just profit?
qs.a: Because a bank's profit depends on the community's health. A bank grows when local businesses and households do well, since they're its borrowers and depositors. It's also the law: the Community Reinvestment Act requires banks to meet local credit needs, and regulators rate them on it. For example, a small-business loan program or free financial literacy workshops build loyalty and new customers. So community investment is a smart long-term business strategy, not charity.

qs.q: How does this business benefit the town beyond its owners?
qs.a: It creates jobs, pays local taxes, buys from local suppliers and gives residents a service close to home. Every dollar it pays in wages gets spent again in town, at the grocery store and the gas station. Local businesses also sponsor teams and events, which builds community ties. That's why helping this owner grow, with a well-sized loan and a solid budget, benefits the whole local economy, and it's a strong reason for the bank to support it.

cards: Everyone affected by a business: customers, employees, suppliers, community, government and owners.
A business's obligation to act in ways that benefit society, not only its owners.
Fair treatment, community investment, limiting harm.
Requires banks to help meet the credit needs of the communities they serve.

pis.title: Types of business activities
plain: Every business, from a lemonade stand to a global bank, performs four basic activities. Production creates or obtains the goods and services the business sells. Marketing figures out what customers want and gets products to them: pricing, promotion, selling and distribution. Finance obtains and manages money: budgeting, raising funds, paying bills, recordkeeping and planning for growth. Management plans, organizes, staffs and controls the work so the other activities run well. (Accounting and human resources are often listed too.)

Businesses are also grouped by what they do: extractors (farming, mining, fishing), producers or manufacturers, service businesses (banks, salons, consultants) and intermediaries such as wholesalers and retailers who move products from producers to customers. A business's success depends on all four activities working together.
key: Four core activities: production, marketing, finance, management.
Finance = obtaining and managing money.
Business types: extractive, manufacturing, service, intermediaries (wholesale, retail).
Activities depend on each other.
Weakness in one activity (like finance) can sink a strong product.
fin: Financial services firms are service businesses, and their production is the service itself: processing payments, managing accounts and giving advice.
The finance function inside any company decides how to fund growth: savings, loans or investors.
Lenders evaluate all four activities in a business plan, not just the numbers.
ex: Cash-flow failures: many profitable small businesses fail because the finance activity breaks down, with bills due before customers pay (SBA guidance on cash flow).
Banks as service businesses: their 'product' is a set of services such as deposits, loans, payments and advice.
Intermediaries: wholesalers and retailers add place and time utility by moving goods from producers to customers.
pis.trap: Don't treat finance as just 'accounting.' Accounting records what happened; finance decides how to obtain and use money going forward. And production isn't only for factories: a service business 'produces' its service.
pis.say: "This owner is great at production and marketing, but the finance activity is missing: no budget, no cash forecast. Our plan adds a 13-week cash flow forecast so strong sales turn into money in the bank."

qs.q: Which business activity should this owner focus on first?
qs.a: Finance, because it decides whether the business survives long enough for the others to succeed. The product is good and customers are coming, but without a budget and cash flow plan, bills can come due before customers pay. That's how profitable businesses run out of cash. So we'd start with a monthly budget, a 13-week cash forecast and a separate business account. Then we'd use the extra cash to fund marketing that grows sales.

qs.q: How does the finance function support marketing and production?
qs.a: Finance provides the money and the numbers the other activities need. It funds production with equipment loans or working capital, and it sets marketing budgets based on what each campaign returns. For example, before launching a $5,000 ad campaign, finance checks how many new sales it needs to pay for itself. When the three work together, the business spends on what makes money and avoids running short of cash.

cards: Obtaining and managing money: budgeting, funding, paying bills, recordkeeping and planning.
Different from accounting, which records results.
A business that moves products from producers to customers, such as a wholesaler or retailer.

pis.title: Types of business models
plain: A business model explains how a company creates value for customers, delivers it and captures value as revenue and profit. Common models include: product sales (one-time purchases), subscription (recurring fees, like streaming services), freemium (free basic product, paid upgrades), advertising (free to users, paid by advertisers), marketplace or platform (connecting buyers and sellers for a fee), franchise (selling the right to use a brand and system), licensing, membership (a fee for access, like a warehouse club), razor-and-blade (cheap base product, profitable refills) and pay-per-use.

Financial services have their own models. Traditional banks earn the spread between loan and deposit rates (net interest income) plus fees. Advisors may charge a percentage of assets under management (often around 1% a year), a flat fee, an hourly rate or commissions. Card networks and many fintechs earn interchange fees, a small percentage of each card purchase paid by merchants.
key: Business model = how a company creates, delivers and captures value.
Common models: product, subscription, freemium, advertising, marketplace, franchise, membership, licensing.
Banks: interest spread + fees.
Advisors: AUM percentage, flat fee, hourly or commission.
Recurring revenue is usually more predictable and valued more by lenders and investors.
fin: Lenders like recurring-revenue models (subscriptions, memberships) because cash flow is steadier.
The way an advisor is paid creates incentives and possible conflicts, which must be disclosed.
Fintechs often use different models than banks, such as earning mostly from interchange fees instead of interest.
ex: Membership model: Costco earned about $4.8 billion in membership fees in fiscal 2024 (Costco 2024 Annual Report).
Interchange model: Chime's 2025 IPO filing showed most of its revenue came from interchange fees on members' debit card purchases, not loan interest (Chime Financial Form S-1, 2025).
Fee models compared: on a $500,000 account, a 1% AUM fee costs $5,000 a year, while a flat-fee planner might charge a fixed annual amount regardless of account size.
pis.trap: Don't confuse a business model with a business type or industry. Two companies in the same industry can use different models: one bank earns mainly from interest, a fintech mostly from interchange fees. Name how the money comes in.
pis.say: "Our client's gym has a product-sales model: pay per visit. Switching to a monthly membership creates recurring revenue, which steadies cash flow and makes the business easier to finance."

qs.q: How does this company actually make money?
qs.a: We'd start with the business model: who pays, for what and how often. For example, a bank mainly earns the spread between what it charges borrowers and pays depositors, plus fees, while a fintech like Chime earns mostly interchange fees when members use their debit cards. Knowing the model shows what drives profit and what could threaten it. For our client, that tells us which numbers to watch, like how many active card users the business keeps.

qs.q: Should our firm charge a flat fee or a percentage of assets?
qs.a: It depends on the clients we serve, but a flat fee is often clearer for younger or smaller accounts. A percentage of assets, often around 1%, grows with the account, which aligns us with growth but can get expensive: $5,000 a year on $500,000. A flat fee is predictable and fair for clients who need planning more than investment management. Many firms offer both. Whatever we choose, we'd disclose it in writing so clients know exactly what they pay and why.

cards: How a company creates, delivers and captures value as revenue and profit.
Revenue from repeat payments, such as subscriptions or memberships.
Steadier cash flow, easier to finance.
A small percentage of each card purchase paid by the merchant to the card issuer.
Main revenue source for many fintechs.

pis.title: Organizational design of businesses
plain: Organizational design is how a business arranges its people, jobs and authority to reach its goals. It is shown on an organizational chart. Key ideas include the chain of command (who reports to whom), span of control (how many people one manager supervises), and centralization (decisions made at the top) versus decentralization (decisions pushed down to managers closer to customers).

Common structures include line (direct authority from top to bottom), line-and-staff (line managers plus specialist staff such as legal or HR who advise), functional (grouped by function: finance, marketing, operations), divisional (grouped by product, geography or customer type), matrix (employees report to both a functional and a project manager) and team-based. Tall organizations have many layers and narrow spans of control; flat organizations have few layers and wide spans, which speeds decisions.
key: Org chart shows the chain of command.
Span of control: number of people one manager supervises.
Tall (many layers) vs flat (few layers).
Structures: line, line-and-staff, functional, divisional, matrix, team.
Centralized vs decentralized decision making.
fin: Large banks are divisional, organized by customer: consumer banking, commercial banking, wealth management and investment banking.
Compliance and risk are often 'staff' roles that advise and check the line businesses.
Fintechs tend to be flat, which speeds product changes; big banks are taller, which adds control.
ex: Divisional design: in 2024, JPMorgan Chase combined its commercial bank and its corporate and investment bank into one Commercial & Investment Bank, alongside Consumer & Community Banking and Asset & Wealth Management (JPMorgan Chase, 2024).
A growing small business often moves from the owner supervising everyone (line) to department leads for sales, operations and finance (functional).
Matrix example: a bank's product launch team pulls staff from marketing, IT and compliance, who also report to their own department heads.
pis.trap: Don't assume flatter is always better. Flat structures speed decisions but can overload managers and blur accountability. In a regulated business like banking, some layers exist for control and compliance.
pis.say: "With 25 employees all reporting to the owner, the span of control is too wide. We'd recommend a functional structure with three leads, for sales, operations and finance, so the owner can focus on growth."

qs.q: How should this growing business organize its employees?
qs.a: Move from everyone reporting to the owner to a simple functional structure. Right now the owner's span of control is too wide, so decisions bottleneck. We'd create three leads, for sales, operations and finance, each managing a small team, and draw a clear org chart. As the business adds locations, it could become divisional by location. That frees the owner to focus on strategy and banking relationships while each lead owns results in their area.

qs.q: Who should make decisions: the owner or the managers?
qs.a: Big, risky decisions should stay with the owner, and everyday decisions should move to the managers closest to customers. That's a mix of centralized and decentralized decision making. For example, managers could approve refunds up to $200 or adjust schedules, while the owner approves loans and major purchases. Decentralizing daily calls speeds service and develops managers, and keeping major decisions central protects the business. We'd write the limits down so everyone knows who decides what.

cards: The number of employees a manager directly supervises.
Line managers have direct authority; staff specialists (legal, HR) advise them.
Compliance is often a staff role in banks.
Organizing by product, geography or customer type.
Consumer banking vs wealth management divisions.

pis.title: Factors that affect the business environment
plain: The business environment is everything inside and outside a company that affects how it operates. The internal environment includes the company's employees, culture, finances, resources and management. The external environment includes forces the company can't control but must respond to. A common tool to scan them is PESTLE: Political (government stability, trade policy, taxes), Economic (growth, inflation, interest rates, unemployment), Social (demographics, values, lifestyles), Technological (new tools, AI, automation), Legal (laws and regulations) and Environmental (climate, weather, sustainability).

Businesses also watch competitors, customers and suppliers. A SWOT analysis combines both views: strengths and weaknesses are internal, opportunities and threats are external. Businesses that scan the environment regularly can adapt before changes hurt them.
key: Internal vs external environment.
PESTLE: political, economic, social, technological, legal, environmental.
Also: competitors, customers, suppliers.
SWOT links internal strengths/weaknesses to external opportunities/threats.
Environmental scanning helps businesses adapt early.
fin: Banks scan the economic environment (rates, unemployment) to set lending standards.
Social trends shape financial products: an aging population drives demand for retirement income planning.
Technology and legal changes, such as new data and AI rules, change how firms handle customer information.
ex: Social factor: more than 11,200 Americans a day turn 65 from 2024 through 2027, the 'Peak 65' years, boosting demand for retirement income advice (Alliance for Lifetime Income).
Economic factor: the Fed raised rates to 3.75%-4.00% in September 2026 while inflation ran at 3.7% (Federal Reserve; BLS).
Political factor: the U.S. declined to renew USMCA at its July 1, 2026 joint review, starting annual reviews and adding uncertainty for North American supply chains (USTR, July 2026).
pis.trap: Don't list PESTLE factors without connecting them to the client. Judges want to hear which one or two factors matter most for this business and what to do about them.
pis.say: "Of all the outside forces, two matter most for this business: rising interest rates, which raise its loan costs, and an aging customer base. Our plan addresses both."

qs.q: What outside factors could hurt this business over the next few years?
qs.a: Using PESTLE, the biggest threats are economic and political. Economically, rates rose to 3.75%-4.00% in September 2026, which raises the cost of its variable-rate loan, and inflation at 3.7% raises costs. Politically, trade rules are uncertain: tariffs changed after the Supreme Court's February 2026 ruling, and USMCA now faces annual reviews. So we'd fix the loan rate, find a second supplier and review prices quarterly, so the business can adapt as things change.

qs.q: How would you scan the environment before giving this advice?
qs.a: We'd use a PESTLE scan, then a SWOT. PESTLE checks political, economic, social, technological, legal and environmental forces. We'd look at current data, like the BLS inflation report and the Fed's latest decision, plus local trends and competitors. Then SWOT matches the client's strengths to the opportunities we found. That makes our recommendation fit today's conditions, not last year's, and gives our client a list of signals to watch.

cards: A scan of Political, Economic, Social, Technological, Legal and Environmental factors.
Internal: factors inside the company (staff, finances). External: outside forces it can't control.
Strengths and weaknesses (internal) plus opportunities and threats (external).
Connects the company to its environment.

pis.title: The nature of business ethics
plain: Business ethics are the moral principles that guide how a business and its people behave: honesty, fairness, respect, responsibility and keeping promises. Ethics go further than the law. Something can be legal but still unethical, like a misleading sales tactic that technically discloses the fee in fine print. Ethical issues in business include conflicts of interest, honesty in advertising, fair treatment of employees and customers, privacy, accurate financial reporting and bribery.

Companies set expectations through a code of ethics and training, and many have hotlines so employees can report problems; laws protect certain whistleblowers. Simple tests help with decisions: Is it legal? Is it fair to everyone affected? Would I be comfortable if it appeared in the news or if my family knew? In finance, ethics are central, because the whole business depends on trust in people handling other people's money.
key: Ethics = moral principles guiding business behavior.
Legal is not always ethical.
Issues: conflicts of interest, honesty, privacy, fair treatment, accurate reporting.
Tools: code of ethics, training, hotlines, whistleblower protections.
Decision tests: legal, fair, the newspaper test.
fin: Financial advisors must manage conflicts of interest and disclose how they're paid.
Sales goals can push unethical behavior if they reward volume over customer benefit.
Ethical failures in finance lead to huge fines, lost customers and damaged trust in the whole industry.
ex: Wells Fargo employees, under pressure to meet sales goals, opened millions of accounts customers hadn't authorized; the bank agreed to pay $3 billion in 2020 to settle criminal and civil investigations (U.S. Department of Justice, 2020).
The Sarbanes-Oxley Act of 2002, passed after the Enron and WorldCom scandals, requires CEOs and CFOs to certify financial statements and protects whistleblowers (SEC).
Many firms use the 'newspaper test': would you be comfortable seeing the decision on the front page?
pis.trap: Don't answer an ethics question with 'it's legal, so it's fine.' Judges want to hear that ethics go beyond the law and how you'd protect the customer's interests and the firm's reputation.
pis.say: "Even if it's technically legal, it isn't right for this client. Ethics come before short-term sales: Wells Fargo paid $3 billion after pressure to hit sales goals led to unauthorized accounts."

qs.q: What would you do if a customer asked you to bend a rule for them?
qs.a: I'd say no politely, explain why, and offer a legitimate alternative. Rules in finance protect customers, the bank and the financial system, so bending them for one person isn't fair to everyone else and could be illegal. For example, if a customer asked me to skip identity verification to open an account faster, I'd explain it protects them from fraud and help them finish it quickly. Being firm and helpful at the same time keeps the customer's trust and the firm's integrity.

qs.q: Why is ethics a business issue and not just a personal one?
qs.a: Because unethical behavior destroys trust, and trust is what customers buy from a financial firm. When Wells Fargo's sales pressure led employees to open unauthorized accounts, the bank paid $3 billion in 2020, lost customers and faced years of restrictions. Ethics also lower risk: fewer lawsuits, fines and turnover. So a firm builds ethics into its system, with fair sales goals, training and a hotline, not just hoping people do the right thing.

cards: Moral principles of honesty, fairness and responsibility guiding business behavior.
A situation where personal gain could influence a decision that should serve someone else.
An advisor earning more for selling one product.
An employee who reports illegal or unethical conduct; certain laws protect them.

pis.title: How organizations adapt to today's markets
plain: Markets change constantly with new technology, new competitors, new customer expectations and new rules. Organizations that survive adapt. They listen to customers through feedback and data, test new ideas quickly and in small ways, invest in technology and digital channels, train employees in new skills, form partnerships, and sometimes change their business model entirely (a pivot). Agile organizations make decisions quickly and adjust as they learn.

Adapting also means stopping things: closing underused locations, dropping products customers no longer want or leaving markets. Companies that fail to adapt lose customers to rivals who do. Today's big shifts include mobile and digital services, artificial intelligence, remote and hybrid work, sustainability expectations and faster payments.
key: Adapt through customer feedback, data, technology, training and partnerships.
Pivot = changing the business model or main product.
Agile = quick decisions, small tests, continuous improvement.
Adapting includes stopping what no longer works.
Current shifts: mobile, AI, hybrid work, sustainability, real-time payments.
fin: Banks shifted from branches to apps; the app is now customers' top banking channel.
Banks partner with fintechs or build their own digital tools to keep younger customers.
Advisors adapted with virtual meetings and planning portals, reaching clients anywhere.
ex: Mobile shift: in an October 2026 survey, 44% of bank customers named a mobile app as their top way to manage their account, more than any other method, while about 10% preferred visiting a branch (American Bankers Association/Morning Consult, Nov. 2026).
Pivot: Netflix moved from mailing DVDs to streaming, and shipped its final DVD in 2023 (Netflix).
Investment in change: JPMorgan Chase spends close to $18 billion a year on technology (JPMorgan Chase investor materials, 2025).
pis.trap: Don't treat adapting as 'just add an app.' Judges want a plan: what customers need, what to change first, how to test it and how to measure results.
pis.say: "More customers manage their bank accounts by app than by any other method. Our plan adapts the bank by redesigning the app first, then turning two underused branches into advice centers for bigger decisions like mortgages."

qs.q: How should a traditional bank adapt to customers who never visit a branch?
qs.a: Meet them on their phones, and turn branches into places for big decisions. In the ABA's October 2026 survey, 44% of customers named a mobile app as their top way to bank, more than any other method, and only about 10% preferred a branch. So we'd invest first in the app: fast account opening, instant transfers, alerts and in-app chat with a real person. Then we'd convert low-traffic branches into advice centers for mortgages, small-business loans and planning. That cuts costs and keeps the human relationship where it matters most.

qs.q: What should this business change first to keep up with its market?
qs.a: Start with what customers are asking for, then test small. We'd look at customer feedback and sales data to find the biggest gap, like no online ordering, and pilot a fix for one month before rolling it out. Netflix adapted by moving to streaming before DVDs died. For our client, a low-cost first step like online booking or mobile payments could keep customers from switching, and we'd measure results before investing more.

cards: A major change in a company's business model or main product.
Netflix: DVDs by mail to streaming.
A business that makes quick decisions, tests in small steps and adjusts as it learns.
Using technology to change how a business serves customers and operates.
Banks shifting from branches to apps.

pis.title: The nature of global trade
plain: Global trade is the exchange of goods and services across national borders. Exports are goods and services sold to other countries; imports are those bought from other countries. Countries trade because of specialization: absolute advantage means producing something with fewer resources than another country, and comparative advantage means producing it at a lower opportunity cost. Even if one country is better at everything, both gain by specializing in what they give up least to make, then trading.

The balance of trade is exports minus imports. A trade deficit means a country imports more than it exports; a surplus means the opposite. Governments shape trade with barriers: tariffs (taxes on imports), quotas (limits on quantity), embargoes (bans on trade with a country) and subsidies to domestic producers. Free trade removes barriers; protectionism uses them to shield domestic industries, often raising prices for consumers and inviting retaliation.
key: Exports out, imports in.
Comparative advantage: specialize in the lowest opportunity cost, then trade.
Balance of trade = exports - imports (deficit or surplus).
Barriers: tariffs, quotas, embargoes, subsidies.
Free trade vs protectionism.
fin: Banks finance trade with letters of credit, which guarantee the exporter gets paid once shipping documents are presented.
Tariffs raise costs for importers, which affects their profits and ability to repay loans.
Currency exchange and international payments are financial services that make trade possible.
ex: The U.S. trade deficit in goods and services was $105.0 billion in September 2026; exports were $321.5 billion and imports a record $426.6 billion (U.S. Census Bureau and BEA, Nov. 4, 2026).

On Feb. 20, 2026 the Supreme Court ruled 6-3 in Learning Resources v. Trump that the International Emergency Economic Powers Act does not authorize tariffs; tariffs under Section 232 and Section 301 of other trade laws remained (Supreme Court; Congressional Research Service).
The average effective U.S. tariff rate was about 6.7% in July 2026, with China facing the highest rate, about 22.8% (Penn Wharton Budget Model, Sept. 2026).
pis.trap: Don't mix up absolute and comparative advantage. Trade is based on comparative advantage: lower opportunity cost, not just being better at it. And a trade deficit isn't automatically 'losing money'; it means buying more abroad than selling, often paid for with foreign investment flowing in.
pis.say: "Tariffs are a tax on imports, and the importer pays them first. For this shop, the tariff on its foreign parts raises costs, so our plan prices it in and finds a second supplier."

qs.q: How do tariffs affect this importer's costs and its customers?
qs.a: A tariff is a tax on imports paid by the importer, so it raises this business's costs right away. The owner then has three choices: raise prices, accept lower margins or switch suppliers. Most businesses pass some of it to customers. U.S. tariff policy has also shifted a lot since the Supreme Court's February 2026 ruling, so costs are uncertain. We'd build the tariff into the price of the most affected products, compare a supplier in a lower-tariff country and keep extra cash on hand.

qs.q: Is a trade deficit bad for the U.S.?
qs.a: Not by itself. A trade deficit means Americans buy more from abroad than they sell, which gives consumers more choices and lower prices. The U.S. deficit was $105 billion in September 2026. Foreign sellers often invest those dollars back into U.S. stocks, bonds and businesses. It can hurt specific industries that lose out to imports, though. So we'd judge it by what's behind it: strong U.S. spending is different from failing exporters.

cards: The ability to produce a good at a lower opportunity cost than another country; the basis for trade.
Even the better producer gains by specializing.
Exports minus imports; negative is a deficit, positive a surplus.
Tariff: tax on imports. Quota: limit on quantity. Embargo: ban on trade with a country.

pis.title: The impact of globalization on business
plain: Globalization is the growing connection of the world's economies through trade, investment, technology, travel and communication. For businesses, it opens bigger markets, access to cheaper materials and labor, new ideas and global talent. Companies build global supply chains that source parts from many countries, and consumers get more choice and lower prices.

Globalization also brings risks and costs. Competition is global, so a local firm may compete with rivals anywhere. Long supply chains can break, as they did during the COVID-19 pandemic. Some jobs move overseas (offshoring), which hurts certain workers and communities. Companies now balance efficiency with resilience by diversifying suppliers, moving production closer to home (nearshoring or reshoring) and keeping more inventory.
key: Globalization: interconnected trade, investment, technology and communication.
Benefits: bigger markets, lower costs, more choice.
Costs: global competition, supply-chain risk, job shifts.
Offshoring, nearshoring and reshoring.
Businesses balance efficiency against resilience.
fin: Investors can diversify globally: U.S. companies are only about 60% of global stock market value.
Global banks move money across borders for trade, payroll and investment.
Supply-chain risk affects borrowers' ability to deliver products and repay loans.
ex: Supply-chain shift: Apple said a majority of iPhones sold in the U.S. in the June 2025 quarter came from India, as it moved production away from China to reduce tariff and concentration risk (Apple earnings call, May 2025).
Supply shocks: during 2021-22, a global shortage of computer chips cut new-car production and pushed up car prices worldwide.
U.S. companies make up roughly 60% of global stock market value, so global funds cover the other 40% (MSCI All Country World Index weights).
pis.trap: Don't present globalization as only good or only bad. Strong answers name a benefit, a risk and how this client should manage the trade-off, such as a second supplier in another region.
pis.say: "Globalization lets this business buy parts at lower cost overseas, but one supplier in one country is a big risk. Like Apple shifting iPhone production to India, we'd add a second source."

qs.q: Should this business buy from overseas suppliers?
qs.a: Yes, if the savings are real after all costs, but not from just one source. Overseas suppliers can be much cheaper, but the full cost includes shipping, tariffs, longer lead times and the risk of delays. Apple, for example, moved much of its U.S. iPhone production to India to avoid relying on one country. So we'd compare the total landed cost, keep a domestic or nearby backup supplier and hold a few weeks of extra inventory, so a disruption doesn't stop sales.

qs.q: How does globalization affect our client's investments?
qs.a: It gives our client a chance to diversify beyond the U.S. Since U.S. companies are only about 60% of world stock value, a U.S.-only portfolio misses a big part of the global economy. Many U.S. companies also earn a large share of sales abroad. International funds add currency risk, though. So we'd suggest a low-cost total international index fund as part of the portfolio, often 20% to 40% of stocks, so our client benefits from global growth without betting on one country.

cards: The growing interconnection of economies through trade, investment, technology and communication.
Offshoring: moving work abroad. Reshoring: bringing it back home. Nearshoring: moving it to a nearby country.
Mexico is a nearshoring hub for U.S. firms.
A network of suppliers in multiple countries that produce parts of a final product.

pis.title: Exchange rates and the domestic economy
plain: An exchange rate is the price of one currency in terms of another, such as how many euros or yen one U.S. dollar buys. Most major currencies, including the dollar, float: their value is set by supply and demand in the foreign exchange market, the world's largest financial market. Some countries fix (peg) their currency to another.

Exchange rates are driven by interest rates (higher rates attract foreign money, strengthening a currency), inflation (high inflation weakens a currency), economic growth, trade balances, government debt, political stability, central bank actions and speculation. A strong dollar makes imports and foreign travel cheaper for Americans but makes U.S. exports more expensive abroad and lowers the dollar value of profits that U.S. companies earn overseas. A weak dollar does the opposite: it helps exporters and tourism to the U.S. but raises import prices, which can add to inflation.
key: Exchange rate = price of one currency in another.
Floating (market-set) vs fixed (pegged).
Drivers: interest rates, inflation, growth, trade, stability, speculation.
Strong dollar: cheaper imports, harder exports, lower foreign profits in dollars.
Weak dollar: helps exporters, raises import prices.
fin: International funds carry currency risk: if the dollar strengthens, foreign returns shrink when converted back.
Banks offer currency exchange, international wires and hedging tools (forward contracts) for businesses.
Higher U.S. rates tend to attract foreign capital and strengthen the dollar.
ex: The foreign exchange market traded about $9.6 trillion a day in April 2025, with the U.S. dollar on one side of about 89% of trades (Bank for International Settlements Triennial Survey, 2025).
In mid-November 2026, one U.S. dollar bought about 159 Japanese yen, near the 160 level where Japan has stepped in to support its currency before (Reuters, Nov. 17, 2026).
The euro fell about 5% against the dollar from late August to mid-November 2026, as markets expected the Fed to keep rates higher (FXStreet; Trading Economics, Nov. 2026).
pis.trap: Don't say a strong dollar is always good for the U.S. It helps importers and travelers but hurts exporters and U.S. companies' foreign earnings. Always say who wins and who loses.
pis.say: "The dollar is strong right now, about 159 yen to the dollar. That makes this company's products more expensive for Japanese buyers, so we'd consider pricing in yen and using a forward contract to lock in the rate."

qs.q: How would a stronger dollar affect this company that sells overseas?
qs.a: It would make the company's products more expensive for foreign buyers, and it shrinks the dollar value of every sale made in a foreign currency. If the euro falls 5% against the dollar, as it did from August to November 2026, a European customer's same euro payment converts into fewer dollars. That squeezes sales and margins. We'd recommend a forward contract to lock in exchange rates on big orders and look for growth in markets where the currency is steadier.

qs.q: Should our client worry about currency risk in an international fund?
qs.a: A little, but it's usually a reason to diversify, not to avoid international investing. When the dollar strengthens, foreign returns shrink when converted to dollars; when it weakens, they grow. Over long periods those swings tend to even out. For a long-term investor, a broad international index fund for part of the stock portfolio still adds diversification. If our client wants less currency risk, some funds are currency-hedged, at a small extra cost.

cards: The price of one currency expressed in another currency.
Floating: set by supply and demand. Fixed (pegged): tied to another currency by the government.
Cheaper imports and foreign travel; more expensive exports; lower dollar value of foreign profits.

pis.title: Major trade alliances
plain: A trade alliance (or agreement) is a deal between countries to reduce trade barriers among members. Types range from free-trade areas (members cut tariffs with each other but keep their own policies toward others), to customs unions (a shared tariff toward outsiders), to common markets and economic unions (free movement of goods, services, people and money, sometimes a shared currency).

Major alliances include the United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement (USMCA), which replaced NAFTA in 2020; the European Union, a 27-country economic union with a single market, 21 of whose members use the euro since Bulgaria joined on Jan. 1, 2026; ASEAN, the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, which grew to 11 members when Timor-Leste joined in October 2025; Mercosur in South America; and the CPTPP, an 11-country Pacific deal plus the United Kingdom. The World Trade Organization (WTO) sets global trade rules for its 166 members and settles disputes. Alliances lower costs for members' businesses but can divert trade from outsiders and create uncertainty when terms change.
key: Trade agreements reduce barriers among members.
Free-trade area < customs union < common market < economic union.
USMCA (2020), EU (27 members; euro in 21), ASEAN (11), Mercosur, CPTPP.
WTO sets global rules and settles disputes.
Rules of origin decide which products qualify for lower tariffs.
fin: Businesses that meet a trade deal's rules of origin can import or export with little or no tariff, which lowers costs and improves cash flow.
Changes to trade deals add risk to businesses with cross-border supply chains, which lenders consider.
Investors watch trade deals because they affect company earnings in exporting industries.
ex: The U.S. declined to renew USMCA at its first joint review on July 1, 2026, which triggers annual reviews; the agreement remains in force and runs to 2036 unless extended (USTR; White & Case, July 2026).
Bulgaria adopted the euro on Jan. 1, 2026, becoming the 21st euro-area country (European Central Bank).
Timor-Leste became ASEAN's 11th member on Oct. 26, 2025, the bloc's first expansion since 1999 (ASEAN).
pis.trap: Don't call USMCA 'NAFTA.' NAFTA (1994) was replaced by USMCA in 2020. And don't say the July 2026 review ended USMCA; it's still in force, now with annual reviews.
pis.say: "Because this business's parts come from Mexico, USMCA lets them cross the border tariff-free if they meet the rules of origin. Since the deal now faces annual reviews, we'd keep a backup plan."

qs.q: How does USMCA help this business that buys parts from Mexico?
qs.a: It lets qualifying parts cross the border with little or no tariff, which keeps costs down. To qualify, the parts must meet USMCA's rules of origin, so the business needs documentation proving where they're made. Since the U.S. declined to renew the agreement at the July 2026 review, it now faces annual reviews, which adds uncertainty. So we'd confirm every part qualifies, keep the paperwork ready and price in a cushion in case terms change.

qs.q: What happens to this business if a trade agreement changes?
qs.a: Its costs and supply chain could change quickly, so planning ahead matters. If tariffs return on goods that were tariff-free, the business pays more for imports or loses price competitiveness on exports. The USMCA review in July 2026 shows deals can change. We'd stress-test the budget for a 10% to 25% cost increase, line up an alternative supplier and avoid long fixed-price contracts with customers that can't adjust if tariffs rise.

cards: United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement; replaced NAFTA in 2020.
Annual reviews since the July 2026 review.
A 27-country economic union with a single market; 21 members use the euro.
Bulgaria joined the euro on Jan. 1, 2026.
The global body that sets trade rules and settles trade disputes among its 166 members.

pis.title: The political environment and world trade
plain: A country's political environment, meaning its government, laws, stability and relations with other countries, shapes whether and how businesses trade there. Political risk is the chance that government action or instability will hurt a business. Sources include changes in leadership or policy, civil unrest or war, corruption, tariffs and trade barriers, sanctions and embargoes, currency controls that block moving money out of the country, and nationalization or expropriation (government taking over private businesses).

Stable governments with clear laws and courts attract trade and investment. Unstable ones raise costs and risk. Businesses manage political risk by researching countries, diversifying across markets, partnering with local firms, buying political risk insurance (offered by agencies such as the U.S. International Development Finance Corporation and the World Bank's MIGA) and including exit plans in contracts.
key: Political risk: government action or instability that hurts business.
Sources: policy changes, war, corruption, tariffs, sanctions, currency controls, expropriation.
Stability and rule of law attract investment.
Manage with research, diversification, local partners, political risk insurance.
Elections and trade policy changes affect markets.
fin: Sanctions can freeze financial assets and cut banks off from international payment networks.
Investors in emerging markets demand higher returns to compensate for political risk.
Lenders financing exports may require political risk insurance.
ex: After Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022, Western governments imposed sanctions and removed several Russian banks from the SWIFT payment network, and about 1,000 companies curtailed or ended operations in Russia (EU Council; Yale Chief Executive Leadership Institute).
McDonald's sold its 850 Russian restaurants and left the country in 2022 after more than 30 years there (McDonald's, 2022).

U.S. trade policy shifted sharply in 2026: the Supreme Court struck down tariffs imposed under IEEPA in February, and the administration replaced them with tariffs under other trade laws (Supreme Court; Penn Wharton Budget Model, 2026).
pis.trap: Don't treat political risk as something only in faraway countries. Policy changes at home, like new tariffs or sanctions, are political risk too. And don't tell a client to avoid every risky country; the answer is usually to limit and diversify exposure.
pis.say: "Political risk can wipe out an investment overnight, as investors in Russia learned in 2022. For this client, we'd keep any single-country exposure small and use a diversified fund."

qs.q: How would you protect this business from political risk in a country it sells to?
qs.a: We'd research, diversify and insure. First, check the country's stability, laws and relations with the U.S. Second, avoid depending on that one market: build sales in at least two others. Third, get paid securely, using letters of credit or payment up front, and consider political risk insurance from the U.S. Development Finance Corporation or the World Bank's MIGA. When sanctions hit Russia in 2022, companies with diversified markets survived the loss far better than those that depended on it.

qs.q: Should our client avoid investing in politically unstable countries?
qs.a: Not entirely, but our client should keep that exposure small and diversified. Politically risky markets can offer higher growth and returns, but they can also lose value fast. Investors in Russian stocks in 2022 couldn't sell when sanctions hit. A broad emerging-markets index fund spreads money across many countries, so one crisis doesn't sink the portfolio. We'd suggest a small slice, maybe 5% to 10% of stocks, only as part of a long-term plan.

cards: The risk that government action or instability will hurt a business or investment.
A government taking ownership of private businesses or property in its country.
A major political risk for foreign investors.
Penalties, such as trade bans or asset freezes, that governments impose on another country.
Russian banks removed from SWIFT in 2022.

pis.title: The global environment in which businesses operate
plain: Businesses today operate in a global environment: they sell to customers abroad, buy from foreign suppliers, compete with international rivals, borrow and invest in global financial markets and follow rules set by international organizations. Multinational corporations (MNCs) have operations in many countries. Foreign direct investment (FDI) means a company owning facilities or businesses in another country.

Firms can enter foreign markets in ways that trade off risk and control. From least to most commitment: exporting (selling abroad from home), licensing (letting a foreign firm use your brand or technology for a fee), franchising (licensing a whole business system), joint ventures (sharing ownership with a local partner) and wholly owned subsidiaries (FDI). International institutions also shape the environment: the WTO for trade rules, the International Monetary Fund (IMF) for financial stability among its 191 members, and the World Bank for development lending.
key: Businesses compete, sell, buy and invest globally.
Multinational corporations and foreign direct investment.
Entry modes: exporting, licensing, franchising, joint venture, subsidiary.
More commitment = more control and more risk.
Institutions: WTO, IMF, World Bank.
fin: Global banks help multinationals manage cash, currencies and payments across countries.
Investors in U.S. companies are exposed to the global economy, since many earn a large share of revenue abroad.
Small businesses can start global sales with low risk through exporting, supported by trade finance and export insurance.
ex: U.S. companies make up roughly 60% of global stock market value (MSCI All Country World Index weights).
The IMF has 191 member countries and lends to countries facing financial crises (IMF).
Export help: the Export-Import Bank of the United States offers export credit insurance that protects small exporters if a foreign buyer doesn't pay (EXIM).
pis.trap: Don't skip straight to building a factory abroad. For a small business, the safest first step is exporting or licensing, which tests demand with little investment. Match the entry mode to the client's size and risk tolerance.
pis.say: "For a small business, the lowest-risk way to go global is exporting first. We'd test demand online, get paid with a letter of credit and only consider a foreign partner once sales prove out."

qs.q: What's the safest way for this small business to start selling internationally?
qs.a: Start by exporting, which takes the least money and risk. The business can sell online or through a foreign distributor without opening anything abroad. To protect payment, use a letter of credit or export credit insurance from the Export-Import Bank. Pick one or two countries with strong demand and simple rules first, often Canada or Mexico under USMCA. If sales grow, the next step could be licensing or a joint venture, but only after demand is proven.

qs.q: Why do investors care about the global economy?
qs.a: Because company profits, interest rates and currencies are all connected worldwide. Many U.S. companies earn a large share of their revenue abroad, so a slowdown in Europe or China hits their earnings. U.S. companies are also only about 60% of global stock value. For our client, that means watching global conditions and diversifying internationally, so the portfolio isn't tied to one economy.

cards: A company with operations in more than one country.
A company owning or controlling a business or facility in another country.
Exporting, licensing, franchising, joint venture and wholly owned subsidiary.
Ordered from least to most commitment and risk.

pis.title: Cultural considerations in global business relations
plain: Culture is the shared values, beliefs, customs and behaviors of a group, and it shapes how people do business. Communication styles differ: in low-context cultures (such as the U.S. and Germany), people say things directly and rely on written contracts; in high-context cultures (such as Japan, China and many Arab countries), meaning depends more on relationships, tone and what isn't said. Attitudes toward time differ: monochronic cultures value punctuality and one task at a time, while polychronic cultures are more flexible with schedules.

Other differences include hierarchy and formality (titles, who speaks first), relationship building before business, decision-making speed, negotiation style, gift giving, nonverbal gestures, dress, religious holidays and meal customs. In Japan, for example, business cards are exchanged with both hands and studied respectfully. Researchers such as Geert Hofstede describe cultural dimensions like individualism versus collectivism and power distance. Respecting these differences builds trust; ignoring them can sink a deal even when the numbers work.
key: Low-context (direct, written) vs high-context (relationships, implied meaning).
Monochronic vs polychronic time.
Hierarchy, formality, relationship building and negotiation style vary.
Gifts, gestures, holidays and meals carry meaning.
Research the culture before the meeting.
fin: Financial advisors serve clients from many cultures, who may have different views on debt, family money decisions and trust.
Banks doing cross-border deals adjust how they negotiate and document agreements.
Multilingual service and cultural awareness help firms reach new customer groups at home.
ex: In Japan, business cards (meishi) are offered and received with both hands and read carefully before being put away; treating one casually is seen as disrespectful (JETRO business etiquette guidance).

Hofstede's research found large differences in individualism: the U.S. scores among the most individualistic countries, while many Asian and Latin American countries are more collectivist (Hofstede Insights).
In many cultures, family members make major financial decisions together, so an advisor may need to include parents or elders in meetings.
pis.trap: Don't rely on stereotypes. Cultural patterns are general tendencies, not rules for every person. The best answer says you'd research the culture and then pay attention to the individual client.
pis.say: "Before meeting this client's partners in Japan, we'd learn the basics: exchange business cards with both hands, expect decisions to take longer and build the relationship before talking price."

qs.q: How would you prepare for a meeting with a client from another culture?
qs.a: I'd research the culture's business customs, then adapt to the person in front of me. I'd learn how formal to be, how decisions are made and what to avoid. For example, in Japan, exchanging business cards with both hands shows respect, and decisions often take longer because of group consensus. In the meeting, I'd listen more, avoid slang and confirm understanding in writing. That shows respect and builds the trust any client relationship needs.

qs.q: Why might a deal fall apart even when the numbers work?
qs.a: Because people do business with people they trust, and cultural missteps can break that trust. In high-context cultures, pushing straight to price before building a relationship can seem rude, and a direct 'no' may never come; instead, the other side quietly walks away. So the numbers are only half the deal. We'd invest time in relationship building, use a local adviser or interpreter and adapt our communication style.

cards: High-context: meaning relies on relationships and implied cues. Low-context: meaning is stated directly and in writing.
Monochronic: punctual, one task at a time. Polychronic: flexible schedules, many things at once.
How much a culture accepts unequal power and hierarchy.
High power distance = more formality with senior people.

pis.title: Cultural and social environments and global trade
plain: A country's cultural and social environment affects what people buy, how they buy and what businesses can sell. Religion, values, diet, language, family structure, social class, education, age of the population and attitudes toward money all shape demand. Products often need to be adapted: changed in ingredients, packaging, size, name, price or marketing message. A product or ad that works in one country can fail, or offend, in another.

Social trends matter too: an aging population creates demand for health care and retirement products; a growing middle class creates demand for cars, travel and financial services; urbanization changes how people shop. In finance, beliefs shape products: Islamic finance follows Sharia principles that prohibit charging or paying interest (riba), so banks offer profit-sharing, leasing and asset-backed products such as sukuk instead of conventional interest-bearing loans and bonds.
key: Culture and society shape demand: religion, diet, values, family, language, age.
Adapt products: ingredients, size, name, packaging, price, message.
Social trends: aging populations, a growing middle class, urbanization.
Islamic finance avoids interest (riba); uses profit-sharing, leasing, sukuk.
Global brands often 'think global, act local.'
fin: Banks design products that fit cultural beliefs, such as Sharia-compliant home financing.
Remittance services serve immigrant communities sending money to family abroad.
Marketing financial products in other languages and cultural contexts reaches new customers.
ex: McDonald's in India serves no beef or pork products and built its menu around chicken and vegetarian items such as the McAloo Tikki potato burger (McDonald's India).

Walmart left Germany in 2006 after losses, partly because practices like greeters and mandatory smiling didn't fit local shopping culture, along with strong local competition (company reports; business press).

Islamic finance: sukuk are asset-backed certificates that pay investors from profits or rent instead of interest, making them Sharia-compliant alternatives to bonds (IMF; Islamic Financial Services Board).
pis.trap: Don't assume a product that sells at home will sell abroad unchanged. And don't confuse 'culture' with 'language': translating an ad is only one step; values, beliefs and buying habits matter more.
pis.say: "A product that works here may not fit there. McDonald's succeeds in India by dropping beef entirely, so before this business exports, we'd test how local customers' values and habits change what they want."

qs.q: Would this product sell the same way in another country?
qs.a: Probably not without changes, because culture and society shape demand. Religion, diet, family size, income levels and values all affect what people buy and how they decide. McDonald's built its Indian menu around chicken and vegetarian items because many customers don't eat beef. So before exporting, we'd research the market, test a small launch and adapt the product, packaging, price or message so it fits local customers.

qs.q: How could a bank serve customers whose beliefs prohibit paying interest?
qs.a: By offering Sharia-compliant products that share profits or use leasing instead of interest. In Islamic finance, charging or paying interest, called riba, isn't allowed, so a home purchase can be structured as the bank buying the home and selling or leasing it to the customer for a set profit. On the savings side, accounts can share profits. Offering these products respectfully could open a new customer group and build loyalty in that community.

cards: Changing a product's ingredients, size, name, packaging, price or message to fit a foreign market.
Financial services following Sharia principles, which prohibit paying or charging interest (riba).
Population traits and trends such as age, family structure, income and education that shape demand.

pis.title: Electronic communication tools in global business
plain: Electronic communication tools such as email, video conferencing, webcasts and webinars, instant messaging, collaboration platforms and shared online documents let businesses work across borders in real time. They cut travel costs, speed up decisions, let global teams work together and help small businesses reach customers anywhere. Banks and markets depend on secure electronic networks to move money and information around the world.

These tools bring challenges too: time-zone differences, misunderstandings when tone and body language are lost, information overload, and cybersecurity risks like phishing and business email compromise (BEC), where criminals impersonate executives or suppliers to trick employees into wiring money. In finance, there are also legal rules: firms must keep records of business communications, so using unapproved texting apps can break securities laws.
key: Tools: email, video conferencing, webcasts, messaging, collaboration platforms.
Benefits: speed, lower travel costs, global teams, reach.
Challenges: time zones, lost tone, overload, cybersecurity.
Business email compromise (BEC) is a major fraud risk.
Financial firms must preserve business communications.
fin: Global payments run on secure messaging networks such as SWIFT.
Advisors use video meetings and secure portals to serve clients anywhere.
Recordkeeping rules require approved, archived channels for client communications.
ex: The SWIFT network connects more than 11,500 financial institutions in over 200 countries and territories for secure payment messages (SWIFT).
Business email compromise cost U.S. victims about $2.8 billion in 2024, and total reported internet crime losses were about $16.6 billion (FBI Internet Crime Complaint Center, 2024 report).
Since 2021, the SEC and CFTC have fined Wall Street firms more than $2 billion combined for employees using unapproved texting apps like WhatsApp for business (SEC; CFTC enforcement announcements).
pis.trap: Don't present electronic tools as purely positive. A strong answer names a benefit and a risk, such as video meetings saving travel time but email fraud requiring call-back verification for any payment change.
pis.say: "Video meetings let our client serve customers in three time zones, but email fraud is a real risk: BEC scams cost about $2.8 billion in 2024. We'd require a phone call to confirm any change to payment instructions."

qs.q: Can our advisors text clients on WhatsApp?
qs.a: Only through approved channels that the firm can archive, because financial firms must keep records of business communications. Since 2021, the SEC and CFTC have fined firms more than $2 billion for employees using unapproved apps like WhatsApp. Clients like texting, so we'd offer it through a compliant platform that records messages automatically. That gives clients the convenience they want while protecting them and the firm.

qs.q: How can a small business manage clients in other time zones?
qs.a: Use electronic tools to work asynchronously, and set clear response expectations. Online scheduling lets clients book times that work for both sides, email and shared documents keep projects moving overnight, and short video calls replace expensive trips. We'd also add security: verify any payment change by phone, since business email compromise cost U.S. victims about $2.8 billion in 2024. That lets the business serve global clients efficiently and safely.

cards: A scam where criminals impersonate executives or suppliers by email to trick employees into sending money.
About $2.8 billion in U.S. losses in 2024 (FBI).
A live or recorded online presentation viewed over the internet.
Lets firms educate many clients at once.
A secure messaging network banks use to send international payment instructions.

pis.title: The impact of geography on world trade
plain: Geography, a country's location, climate, natural resources, terrain and access to water, shapes what it produces and how it trades. Countries rich in oil, minerals or farmland tend to export those resources. Coastlines, ports and navigable rivers make trade cheaper; landlocked or mountainous countries face higher transport costs. Climate decides what crops can grow and when, and natural disasters can interrupt production. Distance and time zones affect shipping times and communication.

A few narrow waterways, called chokepoints, carry a huge share of world trade: the Strait of Hormuz, the Suez Canal and Red Sea, the Panama Canal and the Strait of Malacca. When one is disrupted by conflict, drought or an accident, shipping costs rise, deliveries slow and prices jump worldwide.
key: Geography: location, climate, resources, terrain, waterways.
Natural resources shape what countries export.
Ports and rivers lower transport costs; landlocked countries pay more.
Chokepoints: Hormuz, Suez/Red Sea, Panama, Malacca.
Disruptions raise shipping costs and prices.
fin: Commodity prices, like oil, react to geographic risks, which affects inflation, interest rates and investments.
Lenders consider location risks (floods, hurricanes) when financing property and businesses, and insurers price them.
Supply-chain disruptions affect businesses' cash flow and ability to repay loans.
ex: About one-fifth of the world's oil consumption passes through the Strait of Hormuz (U.S. Energy Information Administration). Supply disruptions there in 2026 pushed U.S. gasoline above $4.50 a gallon in the spring (BLS; University of Michigan, 2026).
A severe drought in 2023 lowered water levels at the Panama Canal, forcing authorities to cut the number of ships allowed through each day (Panama Canal Authority).
Attacks on ships in the Red Sea in 2023-24 led many shipping lines to reroute around Africa's Cape of Good Hope, adding about 10 days to Asia-Europe voyages (shipping industry reports).
pis.trap: Don't treat geography as only 'where a country is on the map.' Judges want you to connect it to costs and risks: shipping routes, natural resources, climate risk and chokepoints.
pis.say: "Geography matters for this importer: its goods ship through the Red Sea. When shipping lines rerouted around Africa, voyages took about 10 days longer, so we'd hold extra inventory and quote customers longer lead times."

qs.q: How could geography affect this business's supply chain?
qs.a: Through shipping routes, distance and natural risks. If this business imports from Asia, its goods may pass chokepoints like the Red Sea or the Strait of Malacca, where disruptions add time and cost. In 2023-24, rerouting around Africa added about 10 days to Asia-Europe trips. Suppliers in hurricane or flood zones add risk too. So we'd map where each key part comes from, keep a few extra weeks of inventory and consider a closer supplier, such as one in Mexico.

qs.q: Why did gas prices jump when shipping in the Middle East was disrupted?
qs.a: Because a large share of the world's oil travels through one narrow waterway. About one-fifth of global oil consumption passes through the Strait of Hormuz, so when shipping there was disrupted in 2026, oil supply tightened and prices rose; U.S. gasoline topped $4.50 a gallon in the spring. That's supply and demand driven by geography. For our client, it shows why an emergency fund and a flexible budget help when energy prices spike.

cards: A narrow route, like a strait or canal, that a large share of trade must pass through.
Strait of Hormuz, Suez Canal, Panama Canal.
A country with no coastline, which usually faces higher transport costs for trade.
Risk to trade from location, climate and natural events.
Drought cut Panama Canal transits in 2023.

pis.title: A country's history and world trade
plain: A country's history shapes its trade today. Past colonial ties often leave shared languages, legal systems and business connections; many former British colonies use common law and English in business, which makes trade with English-speaking countries easier. Past wars and conflicts can leave lasting distrust or sanctions. Historic trade routes and long-standing partnerships continue for generations.

Economic history matters too. Countries that opened their economies changed their trade dramatically: China began market reforms in 1978 and joined the WTO in 2001, becoming the world's largest goods exporter; India liberalized its economy in 1991. Former Soviet-bloc countries moved from command toward market economies after 1991. Experiences like hyperinflation or currency crises shape how people save and invest for decades: Germany's hyperinflation in 1923 is one reason its central bank traditions focus heavily on fighting inflation.
key: Colonial ties: shared language, legal systems and business networks.
Conflicts can leave distrust or sanctions.
Economic reforms reshape trade (China 1978, WTO 2001; India 1991).
History of inflation or crises shapes savings habits.
Long-standing partnerships continue for generations.
fin: Clients' histories shape their money behavior: people who lived through bank failures or inflation abroad may distrust banks or prefer cash or gold.
Countries with a history of currency crises often see residents save in U.S. dollars.
Shared legal traditions make contracts and investment easier between some countries.
ex: China joined the World Trade Organization in 2001, after market reforms that began in 1978, and became the world's largest exporter of goods (WTO).
Germany's hyperinflation of 1923, when prices doubled every few days at its peak, shaped a lasting national focus on price stability (Deutsche Bundesbank history).
Hong Kong, a former British colony, still uses a common-law legal system, which helped make it a major international finance center (Hong Kong Department of Justice).
pis.trap: Don't just list historical facts. Connect history to today's trade: why a language, a legal system or a memory of crisis changes how business is done now.
pis.say: "History explains this client's caution. If their family lived through a currency collapse, keeping cash at home makes sense to them. We'd start by showing them how FDIC insurance protects deposits here."

qs.q: Why do some countries trade more with each other?
qs.a: Often because of shared history: language, legal systems and long-standing relationships make trade easier and cheaper. Former British colonies, for example, often share English and common law, which simplifies contracts. Historic partnerships build trust that lasts generations. Geography and trade agreements matter too. For this business, it means the easiest export markets may be the ones with shared language and similar laws, such as Canada or the U.K.

qs.q: How could a country's past affect how its people save and invest?
qs.a: Experiences like hyperinflation, bank failures or currency collapses teach people to distrust banks or the local currency, and that memory lasts for decades. Germany's 1923 hyperinflation made fighting inflation a national priority. A client whose family lived through a crisis abroad may keep cash at home or prefer gold. As advisors, we'd respect that history, explain FDIC insurance and start with simple, safe steps, like an insured high-yield savings account, to build trust.

cards: Shared language, legal systems and business ties left from colonial history.
Common law in many former British colonies.
China joined the World Trade Organization after reforms beginning in 1978, becoming the largest goods exporter.
Extremely rapid, out-of-control inflation, such as in Germany in 1923.

pis.title: A country's economic development and world trade
plain: Countries are at different stages of economic development, and that affects what they trade and how. Developed (advanced) economies such as the U.S., Japan and Germany have high incomes, strong infrastructure, educated workers and service-heavy economies.
